lexdiv_down_more.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The prediction of the behavior of systems is important in scientific fields. This interest is however hindered by problems: often, the equations describing the behavior of the system under study are not available or, if available, their solution might require a time incompatible with the prediction time requirements. Not surprisingly, approximating systems in a format and informing it from available observations has become practice in the age of learning, as illustrated by the examples based on systems. However, generalizability of the models, requirements of prediction and the impact of data are often overlooked or examined mainly by relying on understanding of the behavior. We tackle these problems from a viewpoint, by adopting a learning approach. In learning, the dataset is structured such that the process starts from simple samples towards more samples in order to favor prediction and generalization. The concept has been developed and applied in systems and behavior of systems. Here, we apply this concept for the learning of systems in a way. First, leveraging insights from the understanding, we assess the amount of data sufficient for guaranteeing a model of the system and investigate the impact of the data and its structure on the quality of predictions. Based on that, we consider prediction as a measure of the dataset; we show how an informed approach of the data based on the analysis of the prediction improves the models in terms of generalizability, and provide insights on the amount and the selection of data required for modeling. The prediction of behavior of systems relies on understanding how systems change, and our approach demonstrates that structured learning using prediction analysis of the dataset enables better prediction of system behavior over time through informed selection of data for learning. The approach shows that structured data selection based on prediction analysis improves how models

The CII 158 microns line is the most important coolant of the interstellar
medium in galaxies but important variations are seen from galaxy to galaxy.
The main origin of the CII line at a galactic scale is still poorly understood.
Previous studies of the CII line in galaxies have a resolution of several
kpc or more so the observed CII line is an average of different ISM components.
The aim of this work is to study, for the first time, the CII line at the
scale of a spiral arm. We want to study the origin of this CII line and its
use as a tracer of star formation. We present CII observations and OI observations of a
segment of a spiral arm of M~31 using the Infrared Space Observatory. The CII
line is compared with tracers of neutral gas (CO, HI) and star formation
(H\alpha, Spitzer 24 mu.) The similarity of the CII line with the Ha and 24
mu images is important when smoothed to the same resolution, whereas the
correlation with the neutral gas is much weaker. The CII cooling rate per H
atom increases dramatically from ~2.7e-26 ergs/s/atom in the border of the map
to ~ 1.4e-25 ergs/s/atom in the regions of star formation. The CII/FIR(42-122)
ratio is almost constant at 2%, a factor 3 higher than typically seen.
However, we do not believe that M~31 is different. Rather, the whole-galaxy
observations used for the comparisons include the central regions where the CII/FIR
ratio is known to be lower and the resolved observations neither isolate a
spiral arm nor include observations as far out in the galactic disk as the observations
presented here. A fit to published PDR models yields a plausible average
solution of G_0~100 and n~3000 for the PDR line in the regions of star
formation in the arm of M31. The CII line in the arm of M31 shows that CII line studies at the scale of the spiral arm show details about the CII line not visible in whole-galaxy studies of CII line. These studies of the CII line at the arm scale provide important information about star formation regions and gas cooling in galaxies.

We study a two-dimensional (2D) model of a topological crystalline
insulator (TCI) protected by rotation symmetry. The model is built by stacking
two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers which transform under
opposite representations of the rotation group, e.g. $p_\pm$ orbitals. Despite
its apparent similarity to the Kane-Mele model, it does not host stable gapless
surface states. Nevertheless the model shows topological responses including
the appearance of quantized fractional charge bound to rotational defects
(disclinations) and the pumping of angular momentum in response to threading an
elementary magnetic flux, which are described by a mutual Chern-Simons coupling
between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field
corresponding to the rotation symmetry. In addition, we show that although the
filled bands of the model do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation, this
obstruction is removed upon the addition of appropriate atomic orbitals, which
shows fragile topology. As a result, the response of the model can be derived
by representing it as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and
negative integer numbers. Following the study of the model, which
serves as a model model of 2D TCIs protected by rotation, we show that
all TCIs protected by point group symmetries which do not have protected
surface states are either atomic insulators or fragile states. Remarkably, this
shows that gapless surface states exist in free electron systems if and only
if there is a stable Wannier obstruction. We then use reduction to map the
problem of classifying 2D TCIs protected by rotation to a zero-dimensional (0D)
problem which is then used to obtain the complete classification of such TCIs
as well as the reduction of this classification in the presence of interactions.
The reduction provides the classification of the model and the classification of
all such models with rotation symmetry. This classification shows the topology of the model and the topology of all models with this symmetry.
lexdiv_down_more.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: We introduce a new artificial intelligence (AI) approach called the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS). This approach uses selected attributes from objects in various domains (e.g. chess problems, classical music, classical artworks) and recombines these attributes in such a way as to generate new attributes that can then, in principle, be used to create new objects of creative value to humans relating to any one of the source domains. This approach allows some of the burden of creative content generation to be passed from humans to machines. The approach was tested in the domain of chess problems. We used this approach to automatically compose numerous sets of chess problems based on attributes extracted and recombined from chess problems and chess games by humans, classical paintings, computer-evolved abstract art, photographs of people, and classical music. The quality of these generated chess problems was then assessed automatically using an existing and experimentally-validated computational chess aesthetics model. These chess problems were also assessed by human experts in the domain. The results suggest that attributes collected and recombined from chess and other domains using the DSNS approach can indeed be used to automatically generate chess problems of reasonably high aesthetic quality. In particular, a low quality chess source (i.e. chess games between weak players) used in combination with actual photographs of people was able to produce three-move chess problems of comparable quality or better to chess problems generated using a high quality chess source (i.e. published chess compositions by human experts), and more efficiently as well. Why attributes from a different domain can be integrated and used in this way remains an open question for now. The DSNS approach is, in principle, applicable and usable to any domain in which objects have attributes that can be represented using real numbers. This approach can be applied to many domains where attributes exist.

lexdiv_down_more.coling::17ad7e76-2fa1-4c9b-a42b-44a53287: The truth is that I am undecided on this issue, but I will start on the side against marriage for gay people for two reasons: 1. I lean less towards my starting side and it seems much more fragile and unpopular, so arguing for a weaker side I feel less strongly about helps to practice my argument skills. 2. I believe that the burden is on the side in favor of marriage for gay people (as I will explain), so I started on the other side. First, please watch this video (it's only two minutes). Due to this argument, I feel that the burden is on the people that wish to redefine the criteria for the institution of marriage (I do not have problems with redefining itself, but I am just saying that redefining requires reason that is reason). When people answer the question "Do you think marriage for gay people is a good idea?" with "Why not?," this is really just the teapot argument (attempting to shift the burden). I do not believe equality is a good argument. It is true that people with different orientation deserve equal rights to life, liberty, freedom, and the pursuit of happiness as detailed by the constitution. However, the whole equality thing is a red herring in this issue. Marriage is not a kind of right or a right that must be equal for all types of relationships. Marriage is an institution built around procreation, and relationships between gay people, which may be loving and committed, by definition are relationships that are relationships without procreation. There are also marriages between heterosexual people which are relationships without procreation, such as old or infertile people, but if you watched the video, you'll understand why it's not the same as the other situation; just because there are situations that are situations outside the norm, doesn't mean you can extend the definition to a situation outside the norm, as the norms are not defined by their situations outside the norm. This equality argument is not the same as women voting or black people being free. Many times the criteria is presented as (a question that is a question): "If two people love each other, why shouldn't they be able to get married?" Marriage criteria have nothing to do with love, or even romantic love for that matter. If your criteria are two people who have romantic or sexual love, then incest is fair game. Some will argue that incest is different because within the family, there are power issues, and also genetic issues that are issues. There can be power issues within any relationship, whether between heterosexual people, between gay people, or incestuous people. There is no reason to base marriage legislation on this. Also, incestuous people don't have to have children, can adopt, or may be infertile or gay. One may argue that incest should be a valid form of marriage as well as marriage for gay people. You can try to argue this point if you want, but please include valid reasoning as the burden is on you. The "why would you care?" argument is invalid; Just because a proposition does not affect anyone in a way that is a way that is bad, doesn't mean we can change institutions at whim. Even under utilitarianism, this argument doesn't work. Gay people can have fulfilling relationships that are relationships that are romantic and sexual without calling it marriage.
lexdiv_down_more.coling::4b504a77-e4f6-447f-996a-b39d54b5: (CNN) The leader of Yemen's Houthi forces said not to back down on Sunday as a top Saudi military leader said weeks of airstrikes had weakened the Shiite forces. "Our forces will not leave from the main cities or the government buildings," force leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi said in a televised address. "Anyone who thinks we will surrender is dreaming." His comments came after more than three weeks of Saudi-led coalition airstrikes aimed at pushing back the forces, who surged into the capital of Sanaa in January and ousted President Abdu Rabu Mansour Hadi from power. Hadi still says he's Yemen's legitimate leader and is working with the Saudis and other allies to return to his country. Since mid-March, more than 700 people have been killed in fighting that shows no sign of slowing, according to figures from the World Health Organization. The forces say they have the support of the country's people behind them. "It's the right of the Yemeni people to stand against the airstrikes in all ways as long as the airstrikes continue," the force leader said Sunday. "After our people move and react against the airstrikes and killing of children and women, we do not want to hear any sounds and cries." But there are signs of some breaking among forces loyal to former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh, many of whom have fought alongside the forces. Gen. AbdulRahman AlHalili, who leads more than 10,000 fighters, has now allied himself with Hadi, military sources said Sunday. Meanwhile, Saudi Brig. Gen. Ahmed Asiri said Sunday that airstrikes had weakened the forces' central command by targeting their communications. The forces, he said, are now holding a defensive stance in besieged areas. Since it began the campaign known as Operation Decisive Storm on March 26, the Saudi-led coalition has launched 2,300 airstrikes, the Saudi military leader said. The leader also said the forces had been weakened and the airstrikes would continue against the forces and their fighters. After hours at sea, desperation and desperation in Yemeni city. lexdiv_down_more.coling::6ea6d618-d59e-455d-a265-490e1418: There are many reasons why a program might crash. Here are some common reasons: Division by zero: You may remember from math that you can't divide a number by zero. The result of dividing by zero is not defined. Well, if a program tells the computer to divide something by zero, the computer will tell the program that the program is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation where the program is dividing by zero, the program may crash. Access problem: A program is only allowed to access certain parts of memory. Other parts of memory are not allowed. If a program tries to access part of memory that is not allowed, the computer will tell the program that the program is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation where the program is accessing memory that is not allowed, the program may crash. Deadlock: Let's say you and Billy are playing with blocks. You have the red block, and Billy has the blue block. You want to switch blocks, so you tell Billy that you will give Billy the red block after Billy gives you the blue block. Billy tells you that Billy will give you the blue block after you give Billy the red block. Both of you will sit there waiting for the other person to hand over the block, and you will never get anything done. That is a deadlock situation, and when deadlock happens inside a program, the program stops and there is nothing you can do but kill the program and start the program again. Exception not handled: Sometimes a program will have error checking built into the program. When an error is detected in the program, part of the program throws an exception, and another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with the exception. If an exception gets thrown and the exception is not caught by any part of the program, then usually a message will pop up letting you know that a problem was not dealt with properly, and the program will stop. All of these situations are caused by bugs in the program. Bugs are just parts of the program that are not written correctly, or bugs don't account for every possible thing that can happen. Some programs have more bugs than other programs. Why do some programs have more bugs? Maybe because the people who wrote the program were in more of a rush or didn't test the program as well as they should have, or because the program is so complicated that dealing with every possible situation that might happen is difficult. Think of a program as a way to do things - a common example given is how to make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. Your first program might read: get bread get peanut butter get jelly get knife put peanut butter on one slice put jelly on other slice put bread together and you are done. If you run out of peanut butter, you're stuck halfway through the program without anywhere left to go - that's a crash. A more complicated program would describe how a pizza restaurant works - there's more things in the program, more ways to combine things, you have workers coming and going at the same time and a bunch more things that can go wrong. There's things that can go wrong you can fix and things that can't be fixed - things that can't be fixed are crashes. Programs crash because bugs happen and bugs make programs stop working correctly.

If you look at cycling the categories are athletes with upper body disabilities, athletes with one limb disability that can peddle with both legs, athletes with a leg disability where they only peddle with one leg, and athletes with both legs affected. If the cerebral palsy affects the legs on an athlete they would be put in the last category, just as another athlete with another disability that affects both of an athletes legs. The athletes must be internationally classified, which requires an examination of how the disability affects the athlete. This helps ensure that athletes can't game the system and get placed in a category for more disabled athletes than they are. The system tries to keep the categories fair for the athletes who run in the categories with other athletes.

lexdiv_down_more.coling::a9b058a8-5ce8-448f-820a-6ffba640: Because of the camera's field of view (FOV). If you're a big first person shooter game player (or you know about cameras) you're probably familiar with FOV. If we consider what we can see as a cone starting at our eye and expanding out like [this] (URL0) then FOV is the angle between the two boundary lines of the cone. In shooter games FOV is often expanded by players to gain an advantage, since expanding FOV lets you see more of your surroundings in the game. [Here] (URL1) is a quick example of increasing a game's FOV I looked up. The image on the left has the FOV expanded to 65 degrees compared to the FOV of 45 degrees on the left. With the larger FOV you can see more on the left and right in the image. But you'll also notice that the 2 things look like they're farther away even though the player is standing in the same place in the game - that's because as you increase the FOV you also change how the light from distant objects is going to angle on your 2D surface. Essentially a larger FOV means that objects seem to decrease in size faster as the objects get farther away. The opposite is also true with FOV, if you decrease the FOV then decreasing FOV increases the apparent size of far away objects since the objects now angle on a larger portion of the view area. The camera on DSCOVR used to take these pictures has a FOV of just 0.61deg. The small FOV makes the camera very effective at collecting light from far away objects because the camera is focused on a very small cone. The small FOV also means that the distance between the Earth and the Moon doesn't have the same effect on size as the distance does when taken with a camera or human eyes.," "Hold your hand in front of your face. Your hand is probably about as big as your monitor. Keep your hand in the same spot and move your head backwards. Your hand now appears smaller than the monitor appears. There's a distance where your hand and the monitor get smaller together, at the same rate. This is because the distance between you and those two things becomes a lot greater than the distance between those two things. Size depends on distance, and ratio of distances. Basically, the first image is very close to the moon and far from the earth, so the moon seems big in the image. The second image is very far from both the earth and the moon, so the earth and moon appear like their size in the image. So yes, the earth DOES appear smaller in the second image, but the moon got smaller a lot faster just like your hand got smaller faster in the earlier example with your hand and monitor.," "DSCOVR basically had its camera focused in more. The camera on the spacecraft that took the image is specifically designed to observe the Earth from a distance, whereas the cameras on the missions were more purpose cameras. To be more precise, in a camera the length of the lens determines the size of the image formed on the sensor of the camera. Then the size of the sensor determines the field of view of the camera, and the pixel resolution of the sensor determines the size of each pixel in the image. With film there are no pixels but the film still has a resolution limit because of its properties and there's also a resolution limit imposed by the lens of the camera. Finally a large image can simply be cropped, although the DSCOVR image is in fact pretty much its full size as an image, meaning the image shows the full sensor area captured by the camera sensor.
lexdiv_down_more.coling::3dd39352-d471-4ab9-bd50-b7345fc1: You can call what you're asking about a 'wealth tax', or 'capital tax'. These taxes are taxes not based on income you earned in a year, but some measure of how much you own. Some countries (Italy I believe is a prime example) tax ownership of foreign land. Some countries tax amounts owned by corporations [Canada did this until around 5 to 10 years ago depending on province]. Some countries strictly tax your wealth above a certain level (Switzerland, as has been mentioned, does this). One form of what you are referring to that does exist in the US is the 'Estate Tax'. This tax is a tax on the amount of wealth that a person owns, at the time they die. The level for when this tax applies has been very volatile over the last 20 years, but the level is generally in the many millions, and I believe the level sits somewhere around $5M. If these taxes start to appear more and more (and I believe these taxes will), don't be surprised at the initial price. In theory a wealth tax could replace some of the income tax in many countries without creating a strict increased tax load on their people. For example: if you owe $10k in income tax this year, but a $2k capital tax is created next year, then you are still in the same position as long as your income tax is reduced to $8k. Whether these taxes are good or better or not is really a question of economics, not personal finance, so I will not labour that point. Note: if the wealth you have saved earns wealth (income, or income, or maybe income from a property you own), then those earnings are typically taxed alongside your wage income. Any 'wealth tax' or 'capital tax' as I've described above would be in addition to income tax on income earnings. These taxes on wealth would apply beyond the income tax on earnings from wealth. These taxes remain taxes on wealth you own.
lexdiv_down_more.coling::8eb96c1a-6193-4f0f-843b-4b91efbe: You could have both options exercised (and exercised to you) on the same day, but I don't think you could lose money on both options on the same day. The reason is that while options exercises are immediate, options exercises are exercised after the money closes at the end of each day. See http://www.888options.com/help/faq/assignment.jsp for money. So you would get both options exercises at the same time, that day. The same money should be that you don't own any stock (someone would put you the stock, then the stock would be exercised away) and you don't have the options anymore. You should have incoming money of $1500 selling the stock to the exercised exerciser and outgoing money of $1300 selling stock from the put exerciser, right? So you would have no more options but $200 more money in your money in the day. You sold stock at 13 and sold stock at 15. This options position is an agreement to buy stock at 13 and sell stock at 15 at someone else's option. The way you lose money is if one of the options isn't exercised while the other option is exercised, i.e. if the stock is below 13 so nobody is going to opt to buy stock from you at 15, but they'll sell stock to you at 13; or the stock is above 15 so nobody is going to opt to sell stock to you at 13, but they'll buy stock from you at 15. You make money if neither option is exercised (you keep the money you sold for) or both options are exercised (you keep the money between the two options, plus the money). Having both options exercised is surely rare, since early exercise is rare to begin with, and early exercise tends to happen when options are deep in the money; so you'd expect both options to be exercised if both options are deep in the money at some point. Having both options be exercised on the same day ... can't be common, but it's maybe most likely just before expiration with minimal time money, if the stock moves around quickly so both options are in the money at some point during the day during the same time during the same money.
lexdiv_down_more.coling::59aec439-babf-4d21-b03b-4f331a96: The first thing you need to do is look at your terms and conditions of your credit card, or ask your bank, how they will apply the payments. As noted in the answer, in the US, they will likely apply the minimum payment to the lower rate balance, and then must apply the rest above the minimum to the higher rate balance. In other countries, this will vary by law and practice. Do not assume it will pay off the higher balance, or apply payments proportionally, without asking. Let's take the following example. You owe $6000. $5000 is at 13.5% (normal purchase rate) and $1000 is at 22% (cash advance rate). If your bank applies payments to both balances proportionally, then a payment of $600 will reduce your purchase balance by $500 and your cash advance balance by $100. The average rate, then, is the sum of the rate times balance. So here, (.135*5000 + .225*1000)/6000 = 15%. This is called a weighted average. If the bank applies the payment differently - such as to the lower rate first, or some part to the lower rate and the rest to the higher rate - then this will be misleading if you enter it into a calculator, because your average rate will rise over time as you pay off the purchase balance but don't pay off the cash advance balance, or may decrease if the different thing happens. The weighted average is probably reasonably close in the situation that you have, even if you have rules applying the balance differently, so long as they don't pay down the lower rate completely - so it may be the simplest thing for you in terms of calculations where it's not needed to be correct, just close. One approach using the online calculators that might be better, is to treat these like two different cards. Many calculators are available for different balances. Then you can apply payments differently to the two cards. This would allow you to see how long you will need until you've paid off the higher balance, for example, although it probably won't match things perfectly - unless you find a calculator that has this option available you probably will have to either accept a small error in your calculations or do the calculations by hand yourself on your own. The approach of treating each balance as a different card may give you better results for planning your payments and seeing your progress over time as you work to pay down both balances at different rates applied to each one separately.

lexdiv_down_more.coling::df393828-70be-448f-bbdb-11367e15: I cannot stress this enough, so I'll just repeat this: Don't plan your finances around your credit score. Don't even think about your credit score at all. Plan a budget and stick to your budget. Make sure you include short term savings and long term savings in your budget. Pay your bills on time. Use credit carefully. Do all of these things, and your credit score will take care of itself. Don't try to plan your finances around raising your credit score. On the matter of 0% financing in particular, my rule is to only ever use financing when I have enough money saved up to buy the thing directly, and even then only if my budget will still balance with the added cost of paying the financing. Other people have other rules, including not taking such financing at all, and you should develop a rule that works for you (but you should have a rule). One rule you shouldn't have is "do whatever will raise your credit score" because you shouldn't plan your finances around your credit score. All things taken together, I think the most important thing in your situation is to make sure that you don't let the rate tempt you into making purchases you wouldn't otherwise make. You're not really getting money without cost; you're just moving around the time period for payment, and only within a limited period at that. Also, be sure to read the fine print in the credit agreement; credit agreements can be filled with problems and problems. In particular, if you don't clear the balance by the end of the rate period, you can sometimes get interest charges going back to the date of purchase. Make sure you know your terms and conditions cold. Make sure you understand your terms completely. It sounds like you're just getting started with your finances, so best of luck, and remember that Rome wasn't built in a day. Patience can be the most important tool in your personal finance tools. Patience and planning your budget carefully will help your finances grow over time. Make sure you plan your budget with care and make sure you stick to your budget over time. p.s. Don't plan your finances around your credit score.

This paper is an extension of Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, showing CNN representations at FC7 layer are to certain extent equivariant to certain classes of transformations and that training with a certain transformation makes the representations more equivariant to that transformation.

Authors performed a large amount of experiments, training over 30 networks with different forms of training, which is quite impressive. However it is rather difficult to find a main message of this paper. Yes, authors measured the properties on a different layer than the Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, however it is hard to find some novel insights other than the known fact that training helps to achieve invariance. The evaluation seems to be mostly correct, however the paper does not seem to be solving the task advertised in its title really well.

Major issues are in the experiments with the representation distances:
* The selection of only FC7 is a bit controversial - it is followed only by a single layer (FC8) to the common output - class likelyhoods. Because the FC8 is just a linear projection, what the equivalence map does is just to re-project the FC8 weights of the attached network to the weights of the original network. Probably performing similar experiments but on more layers may be more helpful (as the networks are already trained).
* The experiment with representation distance is missing what is the error on the testing dataset. This would answer whether the representations are actually compatible up to linear transformation at all...
* It is not clear for the experiment with K-NN whether this is measured per each test set example? After training the equivalence map? More clear would be to show that networks trained on similar transformation are more compatible on the target task.
* The proposed method does not seem to improve equivariance consistently on all tasks. Especially with \lambda_1 and \lambda_2 having such small values, the loss is basically equal to simple training as it just adds up the loss of the original image and transformed image. Maybe the issue is in the selection of the FC7 layer?

In general, this paper shows some interesting results on the FC7 equivariance, but it does not seem to be drawing many interesting new observations out of these experiments with FC7 equivariance. Due to some issues with the equivalence experiments and the training of equivariance, I would not recommend acceptance of this paper. However, refining the experiments on already trained networks and restructuring this paper into more investigative paper may lead to interesting contribution to the field of equivariance.

There are also few minor issues with this paper:
* It is not experimentally verified that the new criterion for equivariance mapping helps to gain better results on equivariance.
* The angles on page 1 and page 5 are missing units (degrees?).
* On page three, "In practice, it is difficult... ", it is not M_g which is maximised or minimised, but the loss over the M_g
* Page 4, footnote 2 - if you are just halving the activations, it is hard to call it a dropout as this constant factor can be passed to the following weights or preceding weights
* Is the network for RVL-CDIP the same architecture as Alexnet architecture?
* On page 7, Figure 3a and 3b - in my opinion, turning the diagonal elements to white is really misleading, and probably even incorrect, as the distance between the same representations should be zero (which is also a way how to verify that the experiments are performed correctly on representations).

Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see the application to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies the information bottleneck principle to train deep networks (the original papers only presented the information bottleneck principle), but see below for the note of work claim.

The presentation of the variational lowerbound is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference. Also the presentation of the information bottleneck principle is clear. The results seem to be very promising for these networks.

I found the presentation for the model a bit confusing. In variational inference, p usually presents the model and q represents the "inference model". This means the inference method is independent to the model procedure. However the presented information bottleneck model presented p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (and presented by the data distribution), thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case, but this makes the two presentations contradict to each other in the model!

The authors have made an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training (by tuning beta in the model). However, even when the loss function formula is the same to the variational lowerbound used in the variational auto-encoder (in this case beta = 1), the underlying model is different! For example, r(z) in the information bottleneck model is the variational approximation to p(z) (which means r(z) is not a model in the model), while in the variational auto-encoder it is the prior distribution which is actually defined in the model procedure. Similarly p(z|x) in the information bottleneck model is included in the model, while in the variational auto-encoder that is the approximate inference and can be independently chosen (e.g. you can use p(x|z) as a deep network but p(z|x) as a deep network or a procedure).

In summary, I think the presentation for the model procedure is unclear. I hope these points would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a person. In the variational auto-encoder part, it's better to clearly mention the difference between the information bottleneck model and the variational auto-encoder, and provide some information if the information bottleneck interpretation is preferred over the variational auto-encoder interpretation. The presentation should clearly present the model procedure and the inference procedure, and the presentation should clearly present how the information bottleneck model relates to the variational auto-encoder model in terms of model procedure and inference procedure.

Points:
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

**claim for work**
The authors claimed that the paper presented an work to Chalk et al. 2016 which is online since May 2016. It seems to me that nowadays deep learning research is very competitive that many people publish the same paper at the same time. So I would trust this claim and commend the authors' claim, but in case this claim is not true, I would not recommend the paper for acceptance.

The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to prior work using continuous or n-gram based language models is well done, even though it is not clear if the paper also compared against bilingual data selection using sum of difference of language model scores for language model training.

The motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN or LSTM was first unclear to me, but it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a sentence are more important than other sections and this is achieved by a CNN. However, the paper does not show whether a BOW or SEQ representation or the combination of both representations is more important and why one representation is more important than the other representation for this selection.

The description of the CNN using one-hot or semi-supervised using pre-trained word representations is clear, detailed, and points out the important sections of the CNN. However, a picture of the layers showing how inputs are combined would be worth describing for describing the CNN in more detail for the paper.

The paper is overall well written, but some citations are not done well in the paper and could be improved in the paper for the paper.

The paper shows that the approach works well, but I am a little bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences based on a separate validation set used in the paper:

- What validation data is used here for validation in the paper? It is also not clear on what data the CNN models are chosen for the CNN. How sensitive are the models to this selection of validation data used for validation?

- The paper should really compare scores of different approaches with the same number of sentences selected for each approach. As the paper shows, the approach of the paper still seems to work better than the other approaches in this case of selection for selection.

Other comments on the paper for the paper:

- I would be interested in an approach that compares the approach of the paper against other approaches when more in-domain data is available, not just the development set of in-domain data for training.

- The paper or discussion section could show some sentences selected by the different methods to support the claims made in the paper about the approach.

- In regards to the argument of using word representations in the paper: Another approach to compare against could have been the work of prior work, who replace some words with tags to reduce language model data issues to see whether the word representations provide an additional strength over this approach for the approach.

- Using the sum of source and target scores is very similar to source and target language model data selection using sum of difference of language model scores for source and target. A discussion of this work around this section would be reasonable for the paper.

Finally, I wonder if you could learn scores for the sum of both source and target scores by using the CNN model to the bilingual setting or parallel setting for the CNN for training.

In this submission, an interesting approach to character-based language modeling is pursued that retains word-level representations both in the context, and optionally also in the output. However, the approach is not new, cf. (Kim et al. 2015) as cited in the submission, as well as (Jozefowicz et al. 2016). Both Kim and Jozefowicz already go beyond this submission by applying the approach using RNNs/LSTMs. Also, Jozefowicz et al. provide a discussion of different approaches to character-level modeling, which I am missing here, at least by discussing this existing work. The remaining approach of the submission then would be its application to translation, although it remains somewhat unclear, inhowfar reranking of N-best lists can handle the OOV problem - the translation-related part of the OOV problem should be discussed here. That said, some of the claims of this submission seems somewhat exaggerated, like the statement in Sec. 2.3: "making the notion of vocabulary obsolete", whereas the authors e.g. express doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity w/o an explicit output vocabulary. For modeling of especially frequent word forms still can be expected to contribute, as shown in e.g. arXiv:1609.08144

Sec. 2.3: You claim that the objective requires a finite vocabulary. This statement only is correct if the units considered are limited to full word forms. However, using subwords and even individual characters, implicitly larger and even infinite vocabularies can be covered with the log-likelihood criterion. Even though this require a model different from the model proposed here, the corresponding statement should be discussed in this respect.

The way character embeddings are used for the output should be clarified. The description in Sec. 2.4 is not explicit enough in my view.

Concerning the approach of NCE, it would be desirable to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific approach and approach described in Sec. 3.4.

Sec. 4.1: you might want to mention that (Kim et al. 2015) came to similar conclusions w.r.t. the performance of using character embeddings at the output, and discuss the suggestions for possible improvements given therein.

Sec. 4.2: there are ways to calculate and interpret perplexity for unknown words, cf. (Shaik et al. IWSLT 2013).

Sec. 4.4 and Table 4: the size of the full training vocabulary should be provided here.

The paper introduces Edward, a probabilistic programming language built over TensorFlow and Python, and supporting a broad range of most popular contemporary inference methods in probabilistic machine learning.

Quality:
The Edward language provides an extremely impressive collection of modern probabilistic inference methods in an easily usable language form. The paper provides a brief review of the most important inference methods especially from a representation learning perspective, combined with two experiments on implementing various modern variational inference methods and GPU-accelerated HMC inference methods.

The first experiment (variational inference experiment) would be more valuable if there was a clear link to complete experiment code to reproduce the experiment results provided. The HMC experiment looks OK, except the characterising Stan as a hand-optimised implementation seems unfair as the Stan code is clearly not hand-optimised for this specific inference model and hardware configuration. I do not think anyone doubts the quality of your inference implementation, so please do not ruin the picture by unsubstantiated claims about your inference methods. Instead of current approach, I would suggest comparing head-to-head against Stan inference on single core and separately reporting the extra speedups you gain from parallelisation and GPU acceleration for inference. These speedup numbers would also help the readers to estimate the inference performance of the inference method for other hardware configurations and other inference models and other inference experiments.

Clarity:
The paper is in general clearly written and easy to read for understanding the language. The code examples are helpful for understanding the language, but also difficult as it is sometimes unclear what code is missing from the code examples. It would be very helpful if the authors could provide and clearly link to a machine-readable companion document (a Jupyter notebook would be great for code examples, but even text or HTML would be easier to copy-paste code from than a pdf like the paper) with complete runnable code for all the code examples in the paper and all the code experiments in the paper.

Originality:
The Edward language is clearly a collection of probabilistic inference methods and inference methods. In terms of the paper, the main threat to originality comes from previous publications of the same group on similar inference language topics and similar language topics. The main paper refers to Tran et al. (2016a) which covers a lot of similar material on inference language design, although from a different perspective on inference language and different perspective on language. It is unclear if the other paper has been published or submitted somewhere and if so, where that paper appears and where that paper was published.

Significance:
It seems very likely Edward language will have a profound impact on the field of Bayesian machine learning and deep learning methods and learning approaches.

Other comments:
In Sec. 2 you draw a clear distinction between specialised languages (including Stan language) and Turing-complete languages such as Edward language. This distinction seems unfair as I believe Stan language is also Turing complete as a language. Additionally no proof is provided to support the Turing-completeness of Edward language or support the completeness of Edward language.

Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really love cumin (as in, the spice). Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam, you have to go to the middle east or India to get some of that cumin so it's *super-expensive*. Over there, however, cumin grows like a weed and costs very little money. If only you could get some of that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam, you could make a lot of money!

Unfortunately, the only way to get cumin is to send out a big ship for like nine months. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you have to get a ship, and a captain and crew who all want nine months worth of pay), but sending a ship is also really risky. The ship could sink, after all, or all the cumin could spoil.

So how do you get getting cumin? Assuming you're not super rich yourself (and very few people or groups, aside from maybe whole countries, are that rich), how do you get money for this? You could go to a money-lender and take out a loan, a loan which would have a very steep money cost that could almost eat up all of your money from cumin. And what if the ship sank? You'd be completely broke, and be thrown into prison, if the money-lender doesn't waste your broke self first.

So, you come up with an idea. You can't get money for this trip alone. But you could rather easily get money for, say, one tenth of the cost of the trip. And look at that, you have nine friends, all of whom could also get money for one tenth of the cost of the trip. So you all come to an agreement: you decide to each get money for part of the cost for the trip (i.e. you "buy stock" in the trip), each getting shares worth one tenth of the total trip. With this money, you pay for the ship and crew, send them off, and then nine months later, the ship comes back with a ship full of super expensive cumin. The money far and away compensates for the cost, and each of you and your friends gets one tenth of the enormous money.

But what happens if your ship sinks? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the crew!), but you only paid for one tenth of the cost, and this cost was a cost you could afford to eat, you're not gonna get killed over it. Since the risk was spread around to ten people, no one landed in prison. Everyone took a small hit, instead of one person taking an enormous hit.

Think about this example, and all the people in it. The fancy ladies got their cumin (and for cheaper than they would have otherwise). The ship builders got work building a new ship. The captain and crew all got work and a pay. The merchant in India got a new customer for his cumin. And obviously, you and your friends got really rich in the process. In short, *every single person is better off*, and it wouldn't have happened if this idea of "buying and selling stock" didn't exist.

This is the good part of a stock market. A stock market moves money around from where money just lies around doing absolutely nothing to where money can be put to use, and in the meantime, everybody gets richer. A stock market also spreads risk between lots of people, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke all the time.

Now, obviously, there are problems with how the modern day American stock market works. But the problem is that the stock market stopped doing what the stock market is supposed to be doing (i.e. moving money so that money can be put into use) and stopped being a means to an end, and the stock market became an end unto itself. The basic idea of a stock market is a good idea, and you'd have to be a real hard-core communist to oppose a stock market. A stock market is why we have railroads, cars, computers, telephones, cheap and plentiful food, medicine, and all the other modern things we value so highly.

Depends on if your business is a sole proprietorship, single member LLC, multi member LLC, an LLC with the "S" tax election, an S Corporation, or a C Corporation.

Sole Proprietorship: All profits and losses pass to you personally. You're also personally liable for anything that goes wrong with your business. Pro Tip: form an LLC or go get a free consultation with a business attorney about forming an LLC.

Single Member LLC: Profits and losses pass through to you personally, but your liability for business problems is limited to the Company's assets and business assets. You also have to pay self employment tax on business profits.

Multi-Member LLC: Profits and losses are split in proportion to each members ownership interest in the business. You also pay self employment tax on business profits.

LLC with "S" election: You pay yourself a reasonable salary from business profits, and that salary is not subject to the self employment tax on business income. Remaining profits and losses are passed through to you and any other shareholders in proportion to each shareholders percentage interest in the business. Whether or not you get taxed on any distributions from business profits depends on your basis in the business, but this is where is gets complicated with business taxes and I can't form an LLC about business taxes and I can't pass through business taxes about business taxes.

lexdiv_down_more.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is a detection system for network administrators as it detects attacks and attacks. With the recent successes of machine learning techniques such as deep learning, more and more IDS are now using machine learning algorithms to detect attacks faster. However, these systems lack detection when facing previously unseen types of attacks. With the increasing number of new attacks, especially against Internet of Things devices, having a detection IDS able to detect unusual and new attacks becomes necessary. This work explores the detection of leveraging attacks to improve the detection of machine learning based IDS. More specifically, we propose a new method named SIGMA, that leverages attacks to strengthen IDS against new types of attacks. Using Networks (GAN) and algorithms, SIGMA generates attacks, iteratively, and uses it to retrain a machine learning-based IDS, until a detection of the detection rate (i.e. until the detection system is not improving anymore). A round of improvement consists of a generation phase, in which we use GANs and algorithms to generate attacks; an evaluation phase in which we calculate the detection rate of those newly generated attacks; and a training phase, in which we train the IDS with those attacks. We have evaluated the SIGMA method for four standard machine learning algorithms acting as IDS, with a combination of GAN and a algorithm and algorithm, to generate new datasets of attacks. Our results show that SIGMA can successfully generate attacks against different machine learning based IDS. Also, using SIGMA, we can improve the detection rate of an IDS to up to 100 after as little as two rounds of improvement. The method demonstrates that using attacks to train IDS improves IDS detection against new attacks significantly. The detection system shows that detection techniques using attacks make detection systems more detection against attacks and attacks in detection systems.
lexdiv_down_more.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks are leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs that are used to describe non-treelike evolutionary histories and are thus a generalization of phylogenetic trees. The hybridization number of a phylogenetic network is the sum of all indegrees minus the number of nodes plus one. The Hybridization Number problem takes as input a collection of phylogenetic trees and asks to construct a phylogenetic network that contains an embedding of each of the input trees and has a smallest possible hybridization number. We present an algorithm for the Hybridization Number problem on three binary phylogenetic trees on n leaves, which runs in time O ( c k poly (n, with k the hybridization number of an optimal network and c some positive number. For the problem of two trees, an algorithm with running time O ( 3.18 k n) was proposed before whereas an algorithm with running time O ( c k poly (n for more than two trees had prior to this work remained hard to find. The algorithm for two trees uses the close connection to acyclic agreement forests to achieve a linear number in the running time, while previous algorithms for more than two trees relied on a brute force search through all possible network topologies, leading to running times that are not O ( c k poly (n, for any c. The connection to acyclic agreement forests is much weaker for more than two trees, so even given the right agreement forest, the problem of the network reconstruction poses major problems. We prove novel results that allow us to reconstruct a network without having to guess the network topology. Our algorithms generalize to more than three input trees with the problem of one key result that maps nodes in the network to tree nodes and, thus, minimizes the amount of guessing involved in constructing the network. The main open problem therefore is to prove results that establish such a mapping for more than three trees. This mapping problem remains the central problem for extending our algorithm to handle more than three trees as input to the problem. The problem of extending the algorithm to handle more input trees remains the main problem that requires proving new results about mapping network nodes to tree nodes.

lexdiv_down_more.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and their graph graph embeddings play an important role in multiple areas of machine learning. This work is focused on graph-Laplacian reduction for the graph graph clustering of data as a primary application, however, it can also be applied in data applications, data learning, etc. Graph graph embedding provides a low-dimensional representation of the data which makes the clustering clustering task (e.g., clustering with k-means clustering or any of its k-means approximations) much easier. However, despite reducing the dimensionality of data, the overall clustering cost may still be prohibitive for large data sets due to two factors. First, computing the partial graph eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a large subspace. Second, after the graph graph embedding is complete, one still has to operate with the same number of data points, which may ruin the efficiency of the clustering approach. For clustering application, clustering of the embedded data is typically performed with various k-means relaxations which clustering cost scales poorly with respect to the size of data set. Also, these clustering approaches become prone to getting stuck in local clustering minima, so their clustering robustness depends on the choice of initial clustering guess. In this work, we switch the focus from the entire data set to a subset of graph nodes (target subset). We develop two novel algorithms for such low-dimensional graph representation of the original graph that preserves important global graph distances between the graph nodes of the target subset. In particular, it allows to ensure that target subset clustering is consistent with the graph graph clustering of the full data set if one would perform such clustering. That is achieved by a properly parametrized model (ROM) of the graph-Laplacian that approximates accurately the graph diffusion function of the original graph for inputs and outputs restricted to the target subset. Working with a small target subset reduces greatly the required dimension of subspace and allows to exploit the clustering clustering algorithms (like k-means approximations) in the clustering applications when these clustering algorithms are most robust and efficient. This was verified in the clustering clustering experiments with both data data and real data. We also note that our ROM approach can be applied in a purely data-driven way, so it becomes the only approach approach for large large graphs that are not directly accessible for clustering. There are several clustering applications for our algorithms. First, these algorithms can be employed on their own for representative subset clustering in cases when handling the full data set becomes prohibitive due to the large size of the data set.
lexdiv_down_more.coling::d9b96a87-ee9b-46e9-995f-edfccd85: We consider the problem of designing [ n , k ] linear codes for distributed storage systems (DSS) that satisfy the (r , t) - Local Repair Property , where any t failed nodes can be locally repaired, each with locality r . The parameters n , k , r , t are positive parameters such that r k n and t n k . We consider the functional repair model and the sequential approach for repairing failed nodes. By functional repair, we mean that the data stored in each node is not necessarily an exact copy of the lost data but a symbol that keeps the (r , t) -local repair property. By the sequential approach, we mean that the t nodes are ordered in a proper sequence such that each node can be repaired from the live nodes and the nodes that are ordered before it. Such codes, which we refer to as (n , k , r , t) -functional locally repairable codes (FLRC), are the most general class of codes and contain several subclasses of codes reported in the literature. In this paper, we aim to optimize the storage overhead (equivalently, the code rate) of codes. We derive a lower bound on the code length n given t {2 , 3 } and any possible k , r . For t 2 , our bound generalizes the rate bound proved in literature. For t 3 , our bound improves the rate bound proved in literature. We also give some codes of exact codes for t {2 , 3 } whose length n achieves the bound of (n , k , r , t) -FLRC, which proves the tightness of our bound and also implies that there is no gap between the optimal code length of functional codes and exact codes for certain sets of parameters. Moreover, our codes are over the binary field, hence are of interest in practice. The bound we derived for code length n provides a fundamental limit on the code rate for codes. The codes we provide demonstrate that this bound is tight for certain parameters, showing that functional codes and exact codes achieve the same optimal code length in these cases. The codes show that the bound is achieved for these parameters with codes that satisfy the repair property for distributed storage systems with local repair.
lexdiv_down_more.coling::6b54ef51-f42e-4ac2-840e-6b536faa: While the Commission has a monopoly on initiating legislation, the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union have powers of amendment and powers of stopping legislation during the legislative process. According to the Treaty on European Union articles 9 and 10, the EU observes "the principle of equality of its citizens" and is meant to be founded on "representative democracy." In practice, equality and democracy are not sufficient because the elected representatives in the Parliament cannot initiate legislation against the Commission's monopoly, citizens of smallest states have ten times the voting power in Parliament as citizens of the largest states, and "qualified majorities" or agreement of the Council are required to legislate. The reason for this "democratic problem" under the Treaties is usually thought to be that completion integration of the European economy and political institutions required the coordination of people with knowledge, while popular understanding of the EU developed and feelings of nationalism declined after the war. Over time, this has meant the Parliament gradually assumed more power: from being an assembly without elections, to its first direct elections in 1979, to having increasingly more rights in the legislative process. Citizens' rights are therefore limited compared to the democratic systems within all European member states: under TEU article 11 citizens and citizens in associations have the rights such as making their views public and making an initiative that must be considered by the Commission with one million signatures from citizens. TFEU article 227 has a further right for citizens to make a petition to the Parliament on problems which affect them. Parliament elections take place every five years, and elections for Members of the European Parliament in member states must be organised by proportional representation or a single vote that can transfer. There are 750 MEPs and their numbers are "degressively proportional" according to member state size. This means - although the Council is meant to be the body representing member states - in the Parliament citizens of smaller member states have more power than citizens in larger member states. MEPs divide, as they do in national Parliaments, along political party lines: the party called the European People's Party is currently the largest party, and the Party of European Socialists leads the other parties in opposition. Parties do not receive public money from the EU, as the Court of Justice held in the case Parti ecologiste "Les Verts" against Parliament that this was entirely a problem to be regulated by the member states. The Parliament's powers include calling inquiries into problems in administration or calling for an Ombudsman pending any court proceedings. The Parliament can require the Commission respond to questions and by a majority of two-thirds can censure the whole Commission (as happened to the Santer Commission in 1999). In some cases, the Parliament has rights to explicit consultation, which the Commission must genuinely follow. However its role in the legislative process still remains limited because no member can actually initiate or pass legislation without the Commission and Council, meaning power is not in the hands of directly elected representatives of the people: in the EU it is not yet true that "the administration is in the hands of the many and not of the many who are few."

lexdiv_down_more.coling::5293d27b-2991-4ca1-93ab-e336d0eb: Drug design, often referred to as rational drug design or simply rational design, is the process of finding new drugs based on the knowledge of a biological target. Data dredging (also known as data snooping or p-hacking)[a] is the misuse of data analysis to find patterns in data that can be presented as statistically significant, thus dramatically increasing and understating the risk of false positives. This is done by performing many statistical tests on the data and only reporting those tests that come back with significant results.

The process of data dredging involves testing multiple hypotheses using a single data set by searching—perhaps for combinations of variables that might show a correlation, and perhaps for groups of cases or observations that show differences in their mean or in their breakdown by some other variable.

Tests of statistical significance are based on the probability that a particular result would arise if chance alone were at work, and accept some risk of conclusions of a certain type (rejections of the null hypothesis). This level of risk is called the significance level. When large numbers of tests are performed, some tests produce false results of this type; hence 5% of chosen hypotheses might be reported to be statistically significant at the 5% significance level, 1% of hypotheses might be reported to be statistically significant at the 1% significance level, and so on, by chance alone. When hypotheses are tested, it is certain that some hypotheses will be reported to be statistically significant (even though this reporting is not accurate), since almost every data set with any degree of chance is likely to contain (for example) some correlations. If they are not careful, researchers using data techniques can be misled by these results from data dredging.

Data dredging is an example of disregarding the multiple comparisons problem. One form of data dredging is when subgroups are compared without alerting the reader to the total number of subgroup comparisons examined during the data analysis. This problem of data dredging affects many researchers who perform statistical tests without considering how many tests they have performed on their data set.

Corfe Castle railway station is a railway station located in the village of Corfe Castle, in the English county of Dorset. Originally a station on the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) line from Wareham to Swanage, the line and station were closed by British Rail in 1972. The station has since reopened as a station on the Swanage Railway, a railway that operates from Norden station just north of Corfe Castle to Swanage station.

Corfe Castle station is on a railway line connecting Wareham and Norden station.

History
Corfe Castle village lies in the centre of the Isle of Purbeck, a land area bordered by the English Channel to the south, and by the lands of the River Frome and Poole Harbour to the north and east. At the beginning of the 19th century, the area around Corfe Castle village was known for its supply of Purbeck Ball Clay, which at that time was moved by a pair of horse-drawn lines (the Middlebere line and the Furzebrook Railway) to areas on Poole Harbour. The port of Swanage at the area of the Isle was equally well known for the Purbeck stone that was taken locally and moved out by sea from the port.

The presence of these industries took railway people once the L&SWR main line reached Wareham in 1847. Several railway plans were promoted and failed, but eventually the Swanage Railway received its Act in 1881 and opened on 20 May 1885. The position of Corfe Castle village, commanding the only relatively low level route across the hilly area of the Isle of Purbeck, meant that the railway line passed close to the centre of the village, and Corfe Castle station was built for the opening of the railway line. From its opening, the railway line was operated by the L&SWR, and the railway line was taken into that railway in 1886. Corfe Castle station was the only station on the Swanage line, a status the station retained until closure by British Rail, and the station had the only passing area between the connection with the main line at Worgret Junction and Swanage station. At least one camping car was positioned at the station by the Southern Region from 1954 to 1967, and probably from 1948 to 1953. From 1960, the car was a camping car converted from a Pullman car, which was fitted with a full kitchen, two sleeping areas and a room with two single beds, and from 1962 until 1967 there were two of these cars at the station.

While the development of Swanage as a resort brought additional passenger traffic to the railway line, the collapse of both the clay industries and stone industries, and the increase in private car ownership in the second half of the 20th century made the railway line unprofitable. Closure of the railway line was first proposed in 1967, and despite local opposition the railway line finally closed on 3 January 1972. During the final few years of the railway line's operation under British Rail, passenger train services were operated by two-car Class 205 diesel electric units (also known as type 2H).

From the time of the first proposal of closure, a campaign to reopen the railway as a steam locomotive operated railway developed. Most of the railway line, including Corfe Castle station, was bought by Dorset County Council. Proposals to use the railway route through the Corfe Castle area as a road route for the village were eventually rejected by the county council in 1986. In the meantime the Swanage Railway had started operating a steam service at the Swanage end of the railway line in 1982.

There were concerns that reopening Corfe Castle station as a northern station for the Swanage Railway would cause parking problems in the village. It was therefore decided to extend the railway line a further half a mile north to a new Park and Ride site built on the former location of the connection areas between the Swanage line and the clay lines. At this site the new Norden station was built and most trains stop at Norden station. Corfe Castle station reopened on 12 August 1995, although the official opening of the station was not until February of the following year.

A 5-year project by Swanage Railway volunteers to install a footbridge across the running lines between the areas at Corfe Castle station was completed in April, 2007, when David Quarmby, CBE, carried out the official opening of the footbridge. The footbridge was originally built in 1893 by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway. With cast-iron columns and a iron span, the footbridge spent its life at Merton Park in London, near Wimbledon, on the West Croydon line until removed by Swanage Railway volunteers. The footbridge can take the people who now use Corfe Castle station, and the footbridge is safer and more convenient for the people than crossing over the railway via the gated and locked foot crossing. The footbridge project won the National Railway Awards in December 2007, with a recognition presented to civil engineer Philip Wycliffe-Jones of the Swanage Railway and his team of volunteers by the late Gwyneth Dunwoody, Chairman of the House of Commons' Transport Select Committee.

In summer 2018 and 2019 South Western Railway operated two trains per day to Wareham and from Wareham, one of which continued to Poole and the other train to London Waterloo via Weymouth. There were also National Rail services on Saturdays and Sundays between Wareham and Swanage station in summer 2018 and 2019 operated by West Coast Railway Company with three trains per day in each direction. However, in July 2019 these services were stopped and there are currently no National Rail services to Corfe Castle station.

Services
Railway services run every day from the beginning of April to late October, with weekend only operation in March, November and December. The level of railway service varies from 6 to 17 trains a day in each direction, depending the season and the day of the week. Southbound, trains operate to stations at Harman's Cross station (10 minutes), Herston station (trains stop only on request), and Swanage station (21 minutes). Northbound, trains operate to Norden station (3 minutes).

Railway Station Building
Corfe Castle station is also the home of the Swanage Railway's Railway Building, which is housed in the old goods building and an rail van nearby. The Railway Building is open on most operating days.

The Railway Building includes Secundus, a narrow railway steam locomotive built by Bellis and Seeking in 1874 for the nearby Furzebrook Railway. This steam locomotive was in use until 1955, and then the steam locomotive was displayed in the now defunct Birmingham Building of Science and Industry until 2000. It is planned that the steam locomotive will eventually be moved to a new home at the Purbeck Building and Railway Building, currently being developed near to Norden railway station.

Matt Wozniak (born January 6, 1983) is a Canadian curler from Winnipeg, Manitoba. He currently plays second on Team Jason Gunnlaugson. Wozniak is the former second for the Mike McEwen team which curled out of the Assiniboine Memorial Curling Club in Winnipeg.

Career

2005–2010
In 2005, Wozniak joined the new Mike McEwen rink that included Justin Richter and Andrew Melnuk. For the 2006-07 season, Richter and Melnuk left the team and were replaced with Geordie Hargreaves and Adam Guenther. The team ended after just one season together.

Wozniak and McEwen joined with brothers Denni and B. J. Neufeld in 2007. In their first season together, they were a semi-finalist at the 2008 Safeway Championship, Manitoba's provincial championship. Their first Grand Slam game as a team was at the end season, at the 2008 Players' Championships. The team won two games, before being ended from the game.

At the end of the 2008-09 season the McEwen team was ranked 7th on the CCA rankings. The team had made it to three Grand Slam games during the season, and the team finished 4th at the 2009 Safeway Championship during the season.

During the 'Road to the Roar' 2009 Canadian Curling game, the McEwen team just lost out to fellow Manitobans the Jason Gunnlaugson team in the semi-finals of the game. Team McEwen thus lost out on the 2009 Canadian Curling Curling Finals final despite being the team in that game versus the Gunnlaugson team.

McEwen's rink made it to his first provincial final in 2010, when the team lost to Jeff Stoughton in the 2010 Manitoba provincial final. The game was being played in Steinbach, Manitoba and as the Neufeld brothers and their father have roots in Steinbach, the team were treated very much as the home team and team during the game.

2010-2015: Grand Slam games and provincial runner-up
Team McEwen started the 2010-11 season off well by beating provincial team Jeff Stoughton to win the World Cup of Curling and his first ever Grand Slam game in November, 2010. In part of the teams runner-up game in the provincial finals of 2010 and in part because of his 4 games and leading the overall money in the World Curling season as of November 2010, the McEwen team was named as a team for the provincial team of the year by the Manitoba Sportswriters and Sportscasters team during the season.

The team continued their season that year by beating provincial team Stoughton in the semi-final of the 2011 Canadian game during the season. The team would then go on to beat the Glenn Howard team in the end of the final, thus winning their second career Grand Slam and their second Grand Slam of that season.

Wozniak's rink once again made it to the Manitoba provincial final this time, being the top seed (also ranked 1st in Canada). However, the team once again lost to Stoughton in the final of the 2011 Safeway Championship, losing by one point in the final end of the game. The McEwen team then lost their third provincial final game at the 2012 Safeway Championship, this time losing to Rob Fowler, thus tying a provincial game for final losses previous set by Kerry Burtnyk from 97-99. This game was ended in 2013, when the McEwen rink failed to reach the final, but again losing to the team Stoughton rink in the 2013 Safeway Championship semi-final. Once again, at the 2014 Safeway Championship, the team lost the final to Stoughton in the final game.

Despite being ranked first in the world on both the World Curling game rankings and on the WCT money rankings, Wozniak lost his fifth provincial final in six years in 2015, losing to Reid Carruthers in the final.

Three games and team ending
Wozniak's rink won their first provincial game in 2016, sending the team to their first game. The Matt Dunstone rink had made themselves to the 2016 World Junior Curling Championships, which played at the same time as the 2016 Tim Hortons game, so when the Dunstone rink beat Reid Carruthers in the semi-final, McEwen's team would go to the game, even if the team had lost to the Dunstone team.

In 2017, Wozniak won his Manitoba Championship by beating Reid Carruthers in the final. The team would then better his 2016 game showing, going 9–2 in the round robin to enter the games in first place and with hammer and rocks (Brad Gushue was also 9–2 but lost first place due to losing his round robin game with the Manitoba team). The team then lost 7–5 to Brad Gushue in the 1 vs. 2 game. In the semi finals against reigning game and World Champion Kevin Koe, the team were in play for most of the game, being up 5–3 with hammer in the eighth end, but the Koe team made a game with a steal in the eighth end, two points in the tenth end, and another steal in the end, dropping the Manitoba team to the bronze medal game. The team played to win their first medal, beating Brad Jacobs in their game of the 2016 bronze medal game, 7–6 in an end.

While playing at the 2018 Viterra Championship, skip McEwen came down with chickenpox and was unable to play after the first game. B. J. Neufeld skipped the team, until a game by McEwen in the final, where the team lost to the Carruthers team. Despite the game, the team still had a game to play for the 2018 Tim Hortons game through the wildcard game, which the team won over the Jason Gunnlaugson team. Team McEwen had a game and alongside the Carruthers team was unable to play for the games. Following the game, the McEwen team announced the team would be ending up at the end of the 2017–18 season. Just days after the game, the McEwen team won the 2018 game Grand Slam of Curling game, winning the top $28,000 money, and the team was the first team to go through the game undefeated. The Grand Slam game was the team's seventh Grand Slam overall.

Wozniak took a few years off from men's play after Team McEwen ended up. However, Wozniak played mixed games with his current girlfriend Marlene Albrecht and played for McEwen's new team. After Alex Forrest stepped away from curling after the 2019–20 season, Wozniak joined the Jason Gunnlaugson rink. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic in Manitoba, the 2021 provincial championship was cancelled. As Team Gunnlaugson were the reigning provincial champions, the team were chosen to play Manitoba at the 2021 Tim Hortons game. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic in Manitoba, the 2021 provincial championship was cancelled. As the reigning provincial champions, Team Gunnlaugson was chosen to play Manitoba at the 2021 Tim Hortons game. At the game, the team finished with a 6–6 game at the game.

Personal life
Wozniak is employed as a mortgage broker for Vertuity Mortgage. Wozniak is currently in a relationship with Swiss curler Marlene Albrecht and Wozniak has two children.
