Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon directed by Earl Duvall. The cartoon was released on February 17, 1934.

The cartoon was supervised by Earl Duvall. The cartoon characters were animated by Jack King, Frank Tipper, both credited, Bob Clampett, Paul Fennell, Chuck Jones and Frank Tashlin, final four uncredited. The cartoon music score was composed by Bernard Brown (solely credited) and Norman Spencer (solely uncredited). The cartoon sound was solely recorded by Bernard Brown in the uncredited. Production number 6125.

Plot

The cartoon follows a male bug and female bug who check into a hotel which catches on fire.

Music

The music song "Honeymoon Hotel" (by Al Dubin and Harry Warren) was originally introduced in the 1933 Warner Bros. film Footlight Parade. This cartoon appears on the film release of that film.

Color process

The cartoon is notable for being the first Warner Bros. cartoon produced in color. It used Cinecolor since Walt Disney had rights to the Technicolor process. There was only one other Merrie Melodies cartoon produced in Cinecolor (Beauty and the Beast) before the cartoon series went briefly back to black-and-white. Later, the Merrie Melodies cartoon series moved to Technicolor, though the Looney Tunes cartoon series continued to be produced in black-and-white until 1943. Cinecolor would make a return in several late 1940s Looney Tunes cartoons and Merrie Melodies cartoons.

Modern Greek art is art from the period between the emergence of the new Greek state and the 20th century.

As Greek areas were under Ottoman rule for all four centuries, Greece was not a part of the Renaissance and artistic movements that followed in Western Europe. However, Greek islands such as Crete, and the Greek islands in particular were for large periods under Venetian or other European powers' rule and thus Greek islands were able to better follow the artistic changes that were occurring in Europe during the 14th-18th century.

The Cretan School and in particular the Heptanese School of art are two important artistic movements in Greece that followed parallel routes to Western Europe.

Modern Greek art can be said to have been shaped by the particular conditions of Greece, the large Greek movement across Europe, and the new Greek social group, as well as artistic influences, from Germany and France.

Greek art and Greek art

19th century

The School of Munich

Modern Greek art began to be developed around the time of Romanticism. Greek artists absorbed many elements from their European artists, resulting in the development of the style of Greek art, inspired by ideals as well as the country's geography and history. After centuries of Ottoman rule, few opportunities for an education in the arts existed in the new Greek state, so studying abroad was necessary for Greek artists. Munich, as an important center for the arts at that time, was the place where the majority of the Greek artists of the 19th century chose to study. In the school of Munich, led by Karl von Piloty, true fresco was taught for paintings on fresh wet lime plaster. During this period much of the art was emotional and theatrical in tone. The most prominent themes of the school of Munich were urban life, rural life, still life, and landscape.

Later on, Greek artists would return to Greece and pass on their knowledge to other Greek artists. Some of Greek artists remained in Munich, the so-called Athens on the Isar. Both academic and personal bonds developed between early Greek painters and Munich artistry giving birth to the Greek "Munich School" of painting. Nikolaos Gysis was an important teacher and artist at the Munich Academy and Nikolaos Gysis soon became a leading figure among Greek artists. Academic art, art showing life, upper middle class art, still life and landscape painting, often representing impressionist features, will be replaced in the end of the 19th century by art movements, art movements, Art Nouveau, which are mainly traced in the work of Nikolaos Gysis, Aristeas and other Greek artists. Early-20th-century art is also represented by Greek artists in Munich. Many of these Munich School artists chose subjects such as everyday Greek life, local life, and living conditions of Greek people. Several important painters emerged at this time. Theodoros Vryzakis specialized in historical painting and especially inspired by the 1821 Greek War of Independence. Nikiphoros Lytras concentrated on realistic depictions of Greek life. Georgios Jakobides devoted his attention to infants and children and Georgios Jakobides would later become the first Director of the new National Gallery of Athens. Georgios Roilos was another leading painter of the period closely associated with the Munich School, especially in his early career as a Greek artist. Konstantinos Volanakis was inspired mostly by the Greek sea.

Other Greek artists associated with the School of Munich were Symeon Sabbides, Yannoulis Chalepas, Leonidas Drosis, as well as quite a few artists who studied in Munich, which included Theofrastos Triantafyllidis, Jorgos Busianis, and also Giorgio de Chirico.

Notable artists of the new Greek state were Leonidas Drosis (his major work was the extensive architectural ornament at the Academy of Athens), Lazaros Sochos, Georgios Vitalis, Dimitrios Filippotis, Ioannis Kossos, Yannoulis Chalepas, Georgios Bonanos and Lazaros Fytalis.

The School of Paris

A few Greek painters studied in Paris. Despite residing in the French capital and following the guidelines of the French Art Academy, Greek painters had their own interpretations. Jacob Rizos was involved with the rendering of female grace, Theodoros Rallis with scenes from the Orthodox East and Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos with art, still life and genre painting. During this period in Paris the Impressionist movement developed, but most Greek painters remained faithful to the teachings of their teachers with only some movements in the direction of this movement. The first Greek impressionist was Périclès Pantazis who, after Paris, settled in Belgium and became a part of the group Circle de la pâte.

Themes-artistic depictions

Many Greek artists of this period also drew upon El Greco's style for inspiration, particularly when creating art based on religious themes. This tied in with the idea of modern Greek art of the period referencing more classical styles, while religious art referenced Byzantine, or Byzantine inspired art. Moreover, an important and often pioneering role was played by Greek artists from Greek islands in the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th century, who exploited developments of the Italian Renaissance and baroque art. As efforts persisted with new directions and objectives, Greek artists emerging in the world during the first decades of the 19th century reconnected Greek art with its ancient tradition, as well as with the developments of the European art, especially those of the Munich School, with defining examples of the Greek art of the period including the works of Theodoros Vryzakis and Nikiphoros Lytras.

20th century

At the beginning of the 20th century landscape painting held sway and the interest of Greek painters turned toward the study of light and color. The dependence of Munich slackened and Paris became the pole of attraction for the Greek artists of the period. In the early 20th century Demetrios Galanis, a contemporary and friend of Picasso, achieved wide recognition in France and lifelong membership of the Académie française following his acclaim by the critic Andre Malreaux as an artist capable "of stirring emotions as powerful as those of Giotto". Later in the century Nikos Engonopoulos achieved recognition with his art both of painting and poetry, while in the late 1960s Dimitris Mytaras and Yiannis Psychopedis became associated with European art. Impressionism was the original influence on the leading figures of the art of the first half of the 20th century, Konstantinos Parthenis and Konstantinos Maleas, while Nikiphoros Lytras associated himself with the groups of Munich constituting the last known link with the series of Greek painters in the great tradition of Munich in Greek art. The further development of these Greek painters led to other roads, but always within the framework of the movement albeit with a Greek dimension.

Gradually the impressionists and other modern schools increased their influence on Greek artists. In the early 20th century Greek artists turned from Munich to Paris. The interest of Greek painters, Greek artists changes from historical representations to Greek landscapes with an emphasis on light and colours so abundant in Greece. Representatives of this artistic change are Konstantinos Parthenis, Konstantinos Maleas, Nikiphoros Lytras and Georgios Bouzianis. Konstantinos Parthenis, in particular, introduces historical, religious and elements that allow the classification of Greek painting into modern art. The same is true with the landscapes of Konstantinos Maleas and the art of Georgios Bouzianis. The period of the 1930s was a landmark for the Greek painters, with Yiannis Tsarouchis, Yiannis Moralis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Kontopoulos (introduced art in Greek paintings) and Spyros Papaloukas coming into the limelight of Greek Art. These Greek painters tried mainly to link leading European trends with Greek tradition.

Notable 20th- and 21st-century artists

The second half of the 20th century has seen a range of acclaimed Greek artists, such as Constantine Andreou, recipient of the French honour, and Thodoros Papadimitriou, an internationally acclaimed artist. Giorgio de Chirico was an influential Greek-Italian painter who founded art. Jannis Kounellis ranks among the pioneers of the Arte Povera artistic movement. Electros Vekris, artist and artist, is the most well-known artist to be working in the field of light, Sound and Motion. Theodoros Stamos was a renowned painter. Takis, Chryssa and Constantin Xenakis are internationally acclaimed Greek artists of art. Other notable Greek artists are Hermon di Giovanno, Varotsos, Dimitris Mytaras, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Fassianos, Theocharis Mores, Dimitris Koukos (1948-), Nikos Stratakis, Steven Antonakos, Kostas Tsoklis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Thanassis Stephopoulos, Aggelika Korovessi, and Yiannis Melanitis.

lexdiv_down_more.coling::4622a5f2-c96d-4ea1-9629-b734e976: (Abridged) The Sloan Digital Sky Survey now extends over a large enough region that galaxies in low density regions can be detected. Rojas et al. have developed a technique to extract more than 1000 void galaxies with delta rho/rho < -0.6 on scales r>7 h^{-1} Mpc from the SDSS. In this paper, we present the luminosity function of these void galaxies and compare it to that of galaxies at higher densities. We obtain a measurement of the void galaxy luminosity function over the range -21.5<M_r*<-14.5 in the SDSS r-band. The void galaxy luminosity function (LF) is well fit by a Schechter function with values of Phi*=(0.19 +- 0.04)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}, M_r* - 5logh=-19.74 +- 0.11 and alpha=-1.18 +- 0.13, where as the LF of the wall galaxy has Schechter function values Phi*=(1.42 +- 0.03)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}, M_r* - 5logh=-20.62 +- 0.08 and alpha=-1.19 +- 0.07. The lower value of M_r* is similar with the work of Rojas et al. who found that void galaxies were lower than galaxies at higher densities but the value of alpha is very similar to that of galaxies at higher densities. To examine this further, the LF of wall galaxies and void galaxies as a function of density is examined. Only the wall galaxies in the higher density regions have a lower end slope. The LF of the void galaxies is also compared to the LF of the wall galaxies with similar galaxies to the void galaxies. The LF of the wall galaxies, the Sersic galaxies and wall galaxies is very similar in function to that of the void galaxies, with only lower M_r* values and similar values of alpha. The value of alpha found from the void galaxy LF is lower that that found from CDM models, suggesting that voids are not regions with a large galaxy of galaxies in these void regions.

topics_down_more.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The reliable prediction of the temporal behavior of complex dynamical systems is key in numerous scientific fields. This strong interest in dynamical systems is however hindered by modeling issues: often, the governing equations describing the dynamics of the system under consideration are not accessible or, if known, their solution might require a computational time incompatible with the prediction time constraints for these systems. Not surprisingly, approximating complex dynamical systems in a generic functional format and informing it ex-nihilo from available observations of system behavior has become common practice, as illustrated by the numerous successful examples of learned dynamical system models. However, generalizability of the dynamical system models, margins of guarantee and the impact of data are often overlooked or examined mainly by relying on prior knowledge of the system dynamics. We tackle these issues in dynamical system learning from a different viewpoint, by adopting a curriculum learning strategy for training system models. In curriculum learning for dynamical systems, the dataset is structured such that the training process starts from simple dynamical samples towards more complex system trajectories in order to favor convergence and generalization of the learned dynamics. The concept has been developed and successfully applied for learning of dynamical systems. Here, we apply this concept for the learning of complex dynamical systems in a systematic way. First, leveraging insights from dynamical systems, we assess the amount of trajectory data sufficient for a-priori guaranteeing a faithful model of the dynamical system and thoroughly investigate the impact of the training set structure on the quality of long-term predictions of system evolution. Based on that analysis of system data, we consider a metric of complexity of the dynamical dataset; we show how an informed design of the training set based on the analysis of the complexity of system trajectories significantly improves the resulting dynamical models in terms of generalizability, and provide insights on the amount and the choice of trajectory data required for effective data-driven modeling of dynamical systems. The curriculum learning approach thus enables better prediction of temporal behavior through structured training that progresses from simple to complex trajectories, ensuring the learned models capture system dynamics faithfully.
topics_down_more.coling::7876816d-0ac2-4404-b2bf-deeaa0b7: The CII 158 microns line is the most important coolant of the interstellar medium in galaxies but substantial variations in CII emission are seen from galaxy to galaxy. The main source of the CII emission at a galactic scale is still poorly understood. Previous studies of the CII emission in galaxies have a resolution of several kpc or more so the observed CII emission is an average of different ISM components. The aim of this work is to study, for the first time, the CII emission at the scale of a spiral arm. We want to investigate the origin of this CII line and its relationship to the conditions within the interstellar medium. We present CII observations of a segment of a spiral arm of M~31 using the Infrared Space Observatory, along with complementary observations of the same spiral arm region. The CII emission is compared with the distribution of neutral gas, and the CII emission is also compared with tracers of the same spiral arm structure. The similarity of the CII emission with other tracers is striking when smoothed to the same resolution, whereas the correlation between CII emission and the neutral gas is much weaker. The CII cooling rate per H atom increases dramatically from ~2.7e-26 ergs/s/atom in the border of the map to ~ 1.4e-25 ergs/s/atom in the regions showing elevated CII emission within this spiral arm segment. The CII/FIR(42-122) ratio is almost constant at 2%, a factor 3 higher than typically quoted for CII emission. However, we do not believe that M~31 has unusual CII emission. Rather, the whole-galaxy fluxes used for the CII comparisons include the central regions where the CII/FIR ratio is known to be lower and the resolved CII observations neither isolate a spiral arm nor include data as far out in the galactic disk as the CII observations presented here. The resolved CII observations of the spiral arm segment show that the CII emission properties differ from those derived from whole-galaxy measurements. The CII emission at the spiral arm scale reveals that previous whole-galaxy CII measurements averaged over diverse galactic environments. The spiral arm CII observations demonstrate systematic differences in CII cooling between the outer portions and inner portions of the observed M~31 spiral arm segment.
topics_down_more.coling::1a16d27a-89fc-4df9-8b4f-cf2532a8: We study a two-dimensional tight-binding model of a topological crystalline insulator protected by rotation symmetry. The model is constructed by stacking two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers which transform under conjugate representations of the rotation group, specifically utilizing the same rotation symmetry that protects the topological crystalline insulator phase. The model exhibits distinctive topological responses characteristic of rotation-protected topological crystalline insulators, including topological responses that emerge from the rotation symmetry protecting this topological crystalline insulator and topological responses that reflect the underlying structure of this rotation-protected topological crystalline insulator. These topological responses are mathematically described by a mutual Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field that corresponds to the underlying rotation symmetry of the topological crystalline insulator. The filled bands of this topological crystalline insulator model do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation, presenting a fundamental obstruction in the characterization of the topological crystalline insulator phase. However, this Wannier obstruction can be removed upon the addition of appropriate atomic orbitals to the model, which reveals that the topology is of the fragile type rather than being stable. The fragile nature of the topology in this topological crystalline insulator implies that the response properties can be derived by representing the model as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and negative integer coefficients, where these atomic orbitals restore the Wannier representation that was obstructed in the original topological crystalline insulator. This prototypical two-dimensional topological crystalline insulator protected by rotation symmetry serves to illustrate general principles applicable to all topological crystalline insulators protected by point group symmetries. We demonstrate that dimensional reduction techniques can map the problem of classifying two-dimensional topological crystalline insulators protected by rotation to a lower-dimensional problem, and this mapping enables us to obtain the complete classification of such rotation-protected topological crystalline insulators as well as the modification of this classification.
topics_down_more.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: We introduce a new artificial intelligence approach for chess problem composition called the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS). It uses selected attributes from chess positions and recombines them in such a way as to generate new chess attributes that can then be used to create novel chess problems of creative value to chess enthusiasts and composers. This allows some of the burden of chess problem composition to be passed from human chess composers to automated chess composition systems. The approach was tested extensively in chess problem composition. We used it to automatically compose numerous sets of chess problems based on attributes extracted and recombined from existing chess problems and existing chess problems already created by others. The quality of these generated chess problems was then assessed automatically using an existing computational chess aesthetics model designed specifically for evaluating chess problem quality. The computer-generated chess problems were also assessed using the same chess problem evaluation approach that had been applied to the automatically generated chess problems mentioned earlier. The results suggest that chess attributes collected and recombined from different chess sources using the DSNS approach can indeed be used to automatically generate chess problems of reasonably high aesthetic quality according to established chess aesthetic principles. In particular, one chess source consisting of certain chess problem sequences was able to produce three-move chess problems of comparable quality or better to those generated using another chess source consisting of different chess compositions, and the first chess source proved more efficient as well in generating acceptable chess problems. Why certain chess information sources prove more productive than others for automated chess problem generation remains an open question requiring further chess composition research using the DSNS approach for chess problem composition. The DSNS approach is, in principle, scalable to generating additional chess problems through continued application of the chess attribute extraction and recombination methodology.
topics_down_more.coling::28a6b262-a893-4fcb-a538-fc9aa5ad: The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak position in the cosmic matter distribution provides a standard ruler for measuring cosmological distances at various redshifts. Current BAO measurements achieve approximately 1% accuracy when using galaxy clustering data, and approximately 1.4-1.6% precision when employing Ly-alpha forest observations combined with quasar clustering patterns. The BAO feature serves as a powerful cosmological probe because it represents a fixed comoving scale imprinted during the early universe that can be observed across multiple redshift ranges. The Alcock-Paczyński effect, which manifests in BAO measurements through distortions of the clustering pattern, provides additional constraining power by revealing geometric properties encoded in the ratio of perpendicular to parallel clustering scales. This work analyzes five BAO peak position measurements obtained from the final data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV, spanning average redshifts of 0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48, and 2.33. The BAO measurements at these redshifts enable tests of cosmological scenarios through two distinct diagnostic approaches based on the BAO signal. The first diagnostic employs the Alcock-Paczyński test applied to BAO measurements, which favors the R_h=ct cosmological model over the standard Lambda-CDM model with approximately 75% likelihood versus 25% likelihood. The second diagnostic uses another approach derived from BAO data assuming a constant comoving sound horizon scale related to the BAO feature, which favors the Planck-Lambda-CDM model over R_h=ct with approximately 80% likelihood versus 20% likelihood. When both BAO-based diagnostics are combined in a joint analysis of these same BAO measurements, the outcome proves inconclusive, yielding comparable likelihoods for both cosmological models under consideration. These BAO results therefore cannot independently confirm cosmological scenarios without incorporating additional observational probes beyond the BAO measurements themselves, meaning the BAO peak position measurements require supplementary data.
topics_down_more.coling::f4961832-eeb4-41fc-8a64-82c30107: Let me preface this by saying that I really do like Cowboy Bebop's characters in theory, but in execution they present significant problems that undermine the show's overall quality. I'll start with the core ensemble, which is where many of my issues originate. While I'll admit that Spike and Jet are genuinely well-developed characters with compelling backstories, meaningful arcs, and excellent chemistry, they represent only two-fifths of the entire Bebop crew, and the remaining three characters suffer from various degrees of underdevelopment and problematic writing choices that prevent them from achieving the same level of depth and complexity that Spike and Jet demonstrate throughout the series. Ein's introduction initially suggests he will be a meaningful participant in the crew's adventures, but this premise goes absolutely nowhere and he spends the remainder of the show simply existing alongside the other crew members, occasionally appearing in scenes but never developing beyond his initial characterization or contributing meaningfully to the narrative in ways that justify his presence among the main cast. Faye exhibits many of the worst characteristics that can be written about a female character; she's bossy without justification, greedy to a fault, obsessed with her own appearance, needs to either be rescued by the other characters or serves as a hindrance to the group more often than she functions as an asset to their operations, and her characterization frequently prioritizes superficial elements over meaningful character development. While her backstory subplot has potential, it arrives too late and receives too little exploration to redeem her characterization or provide the depth that Spike and Jet receive throughout the series. Ed walks the line between endearing and annoying, sometimes succeeding but often becoming grating, and she hardly receives any meaningful character development beyond her introductory episode, remaining essentially the same throughout her time on the Bebop without the growth or depth that would make her as compelling as Spike and Jet. The main antagonist is especially problematic from a characterization standpoint. He possesses very little discernible personality and his motivation never extends beyond vague desires that the show fails to adequately develop or explore. Even though the show dedicates portions of several episodes to exploring his backstory and his previous relationships with other characters, it never establishes clear, compelling motivation for his actions or explains what drives his behavior beyond shallow justifications. By the show's conclusion, he remains little more than a stock villain—an antagonist with sufficient abilities that he can challenge the protagonist in their confrontations, functioning primarily as a representation of past conflicts rather than as a fully realized character with understandable goals and relatable human dimensions that would make him as developed as Spike and Jet. This shallow characterization significantly weakens the emotional impact of their final confrontation and undermines the narrative weight the show attempts to create. As a result, the episodes that involve this antagonist directly don't deliver the emotional weight or narrative satisfaction that the show clearly wants the audience to experience, because the central conflict lacks the character depth necessary to make viewers truly invested in the outcome of the protagonist's struggle, unlike the compelling characterization that Spike and Jet receive throughout the series.
topics_down_more.coling::2b392f9b-db4c-468a-bf65-fc00202e: My reasoning is this: Russia's economy to start with was horrible after the fall of the Soviet Union. To compound this issue, Russia's economic situation deteriorated further due to the economic pressures that have been applied over the years. With the Russian economy tanked, Putin has one or two options from my view. First, he has to watch Russia's economy slowly die, or second, he does something about Russia's economic situation, to try to help Russia's economy. The way that Russia gained massive economic power previously was through the economic resources the other countries held, and by taking those countries over, Russia gained economic power and economic leverage. So to gain some economic power or leverage in the horrendous Russian economy, Putin goes after the Ukraine, because he doesn't want to watch Russia's economy die slowly. This is not to say that it is a perfect economic decision, or the one I would make concerning Russia's economy; but that it is both a justified and unjustifiable position regarding Russia's economic future. The justification being that he doesn't want to see Russia's economy die, but the unjustification being that trying to fix Russia's economic problems through taking other countries shouldn't be acceptable when it comes to Russia's economic problems. Russia's economic challenges stem from the post-Soviet transition, and Russia's economic infrastructure never fully recovered from the post-Soviet transition. The Russian economy faces the same weaknesses that limit Russia's economic growth potential that it has always faced. Putin views Russia's economic weakness as a threat to Russia's economic sovereignty and Russia's economic future. Russia's economic strategy remains focused on Russia's economic survival and Russia's economic power.
topics_down_more.coling::3bec38ad-9c98-4004-95a3-5b24858e: I live in New Zealand, and we are currently in the middle of "one of the most important elections in our country's history" (apparently), and I am not planning to vote, and I think that the campaigns that the electoral commission are running to encourage everyone to vote are stupid. topics_down_more.coling::17ad7e76-2fa1-4c9b-a42b-44a53287: The truth is that I am actually undecided on the question of gay marriage, but I will start on the side against gay marriage for two reasons: 1. I lean less towards my starting side and it seems much more fragile and unpopular, so advocating for a weaker position I feel less strongly about helps to practice my argument articulation skills. 2. I believe that the burden of proof is on the side in favor of gay marriage (as I will explain), so I started on the other side. First, please watch [this video] (it's only two minutes). Due to this argument, I feel that the burden of proof is on the people that wish to redefine the criteria for the institution of marriage (I do not have problems with redefinition itself, but I am just saying that redefinition requires compelling reason). When people answer the question "Do you think gay marriage is a good idea?" with "Why not?," this is really just shifting the burden of proof back to those questioning gay marriage. I do not believe equality is a good argument for gay marriage. Marriage is not a kind of privilege or a right that must be equal for all types of relationships. Marriage is an institution built around procreation, and homosexual relationships, which may be loving and committed, by definition are non-procreational. There are also heterosexual marriages which are non-procreational, but if you watched the video, you'll understand why it's not analogous to gay marriage; just because there are exceptions to the norm in marriage, doesn't mean you can extend the definition of marriage to a non-norm, as the norms of marriage are not defined by their exceptions. The norms of marriage exist independently of exceptional cases that don't conform to those norms regarding procreation. Many times the criteria for gay marriage is presented as (a posed question): "If two people love each other, why shouldn't they be able to get married?" Marriage criteria have nothing to do with love, or even romantic love for that matter. If your criteria for marriage are two individuals who have romantic love, then the question of gay marriage opens other questions about marriage criteria. The burden of proof remains on those seeking to redefine marriage around love rather than procreation. The "why would you care?" argument is invalid regarding gay marriage; Just because a proposition does not affect anyone adversely, doesn't mean we can change institutions like marriage at whim. This argument attempts to shift the burden of proof away from those advocating change to marriage. People can have fulfilling long-term relationships without calling it marriage. Redefining marriage for one group raises questions about what marriage fundamentally is and what purposes it serves. The burden of proof lies with those who want to change the traditional definition of marriage to accommodate gay marriage. Most arguments for gay marriage are appeals to emotion or popularity rather than addressing the burden of proof. The terminology around gay marriage was designed to make opposition seem unreasonable. Just because the issue of gay marriage is popular, and many of the opponents of gay marriage use weak arguments, doesn't make the other side correct about gay marriage or relieve them of the burden of proof regarding marriage redefinition. Why is one approach to marriage relationships more valid than another when we discuss gay marriage? The debate over gay marriage ultimately comes down to what we believe marriage is for and whether gay marriage fits that definition. If marriage exists primarily for procreation, then gay marriage doesn't fit. If marriage exists for other purposes beyond procreation, then gay marriage might fit those purposes. The question of gay marriage forces us to articulate what marriage means and why society recognizes marriage at all. Those who support gay marriage must explain why the traditional definition of marriage should be expanded and must meet their burden of proof. Those who oppose gay marriage must explain why the traditional definition should be maintained. The gay marriage debate is fundamentally about the nature and purpose of marriage itself and where the burden of proof lies. View changed. In all fairness, I was already 75 percent there when I wrote this about gay marriage.
topics_down_more.coling::4b504a77-e4f6-447f-996a-b39d54b5: (CNN) The leader of Yemen's Houthi rebels vowed not to back down on Sunday as a top Saudi military official claimed weeks of airstrikes had significantly weakened the Shiite group. "Our fighters will not evacuate from the main cities or the government institutions," rebel leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi said in a televised address. "Anyone who thinks we will surrender is dreaming." His comments came after more than three weeks of Saudi-led coalition bombings aimed at pushing back the Houthis, who surged into the capital of Sanaa in January and seized control of government facilities. The Houthis consolidated their hold on key territories throughout the capital and surrounding regions. Since mid-March, the Houthis have maintained their positions despite sustained bombardment, continuing to control major urban centers and strategic locations. There are many reasons why a program might crash. Here are some common ones: Division by zero: When a program tells the computer to divide something by zero, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, it may crash. The program should have been written to check for zero before attempting division, but if that check is missing, a crash occurs. Some programming languages will automatically catch this error and allow the program to continue, but others will simply terminate the program immediately when division by zero is attempted. Division by zero represents a situation where the program is doing something wrong and the computer notifies the program of this problem.

Access violation: A program is only allowed to access certain parts of memory. Other parts are off-limits. If a program tries to access part of memory that is off-limits, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, it may crash. Access violations happen when a program tries to use memory that is off-limits, or when it attempts to access memory locations that the program is not allowed to touch.

Deadlock: A deadlock happens when part of the program is waiting for another part to finish, but that other part is also waiting for the first part to finish. Both parts will sit there forever waiting for the other to complete, and the program freezes up. When this happens inside a program, there is nothing you can do except kill the program and start it again. Deadlock represents a situation where parts of the program wait for each other and the program freezes up as a result.

Unhandled exception: Sometimes a program will have a special sort of error checking built into it. When an error is detected, part of the program throws an exception, and another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with it. If an exception gets thrown and is not caught by any part of the program, then usually a dialog will pop up letting you know that a problem was not dealt with properly, and the program will terminate. An unhandled exception occurs when error checking detects a problem but no part of the program catches and deals with that exception.

All of these situations are caused by bugs in the program. Bugs are just parts of the program that are not written correctly, or don't account for every possible thing that can happen. Some programs have more bugs than other programs. Maybe the people who wrote the program were in more of a rush or didn't test it as well as they should have. Maybe the program is so complicated that it is difficult to deal with every possible situation that might arise. Bugs are parts of the program that are not written correctly. These bugs cause the program to crash when certain situations occur. Division by zero causes crashes when the program doesn't check for zero. Access violations cause crashes when the program accesses memory that is off-limits. Deadlock causes crashes when parts of the program wait for each other. Unhandled exceptions cause crashes when error checking detects problems that are not caught and dealt with properly by the program.
topics_down_more.coling::37e384a6-d2b8-444e-ac7f-d4288c17: Paralympic classification systems group athletes based on the functional impact of their disabilities rather than the specific medical diagnoses. The classification process examines how a disability affects an athlete's ability to perform in their particular sport. Each sport has developed its own classification system that reflects the specific physical demands of that sport. Cycling classifications, for example, divide athletes according to functional capacity: athletes with upper body limitations compete in one category, while athletes with single-limb disabilities who retain bilateral leg function compete in another category. Athletes who can pedal with only one leg due to unilateral lower limb impairment form a separate classification group. Athletes with bilateral lower limb involvement, regardless of whether that involvement stems from different underlying conditions affecting both legs, compete together in yet another classification category based on their functional capacity. The classification process requires international certification through formal evaluation procedures. These evaluations assess the functional limitations that result from each athlete's disability. Trained classifiers conduct physical examinations and functional assessments to determine the appropriate competition category for each athlete based on functional capacity. The classification system aims to ensure fair competition by grouping athletes with similar functional abilities together. The system also prevents athletes from misrepresenting their capabilities to gain competitive advantages by entering categories designed for athletes with more significant functional impairments. When athlete numbers are insufficient to fill separate races for each classification, organizers sometimes combine similar classifications in the same event while maintaining separate scoring within each category. This consolidation practice allows competitions to proceed even with limited participant numbers in individual classifications based on functional capacity. The approach ensures that athletes with comparable functional abilities compete against one another for medals and rankings despite sharing the track or course with athletes from adjacent classification categories. Paralympic classification ultimately seeks to balance the goals of fair competition, adequate participation numbers, and practical event management within the Paralympic sports system by grouping athletes according to functional capacity.

Playing dead operates through predator psychology rather than any conscious deception. When prey animals cease movement, they trigger a shift in predator instincts that governs whether the predator continues its attack or disengages entirely. The predator's response depends fundamentally on what type of threat response initially motivated its aggression toward the prey.

Predators attacking from territorial or defensive instincts lose interest once movement stops because movement itself signals the presence of a threat requiring neutralization. When the prey goes still, the predator's brain registers that the immediate crisis has passed, and the defensive drive that powered the attack diminishes rapidly. The predator experiences a reduction in the physiological arousal that accompanied its defensive state, and without continued movement to sustain that arousal, the predator's attention shifts away from the now-motionless prey. This pattern demonstrates how playing dead proves effective against predators motivated by territorial or defensive instincts, as these predators cease their attacks when movement stops signaling threat.

Predators hunting for food, however, respond to stillness differently because their motivation centers on obtaining a meal rather than eliminating a perceived threat. These predators possess instincts calibrated to movement as a trigger for attack behaviors, but once attack occurs, stillness does not signal safety to the predator. Instead, the predator transitions from attack mode into feeding mode. The prey's immobility actually facilitates consumption rather than discouraging it. Predators motivated by hunger exemplify this pattern: they attack to eat, and when struggling ceases, they interpret this as the appropriate moment to begin feeding rather than as a reason to withdraw.

The effectiveness of death feigning therefore depends entirely on correctly assessing the predator's underlying motivation. Against a predator defending territory or reacting to perceived danger, immobility can deactivate the aggressive response by removing the movement cues that maintain defensive arousal. Against a predator hunting for sustenance, immobility fails because the predator's instinctive sequence proceeds directly from successful attack to consumption, with stillness serving as the signal to transition between these phases rather than to abandon the interaction entirely.
topics_down_more.coling::a9b058a8-5ce8-448f-820a-6ffba640: Because of the camera's field of view (FOV). The field of view represents the angular extent of the observable area that a camera can capture at any given moment. If we consider what a camera can see as a cone starting at the lens and expanding outward, then FOV is the angle between the two boundary lines of that cone. The field of view fundamentally determines how much of a scene the camera will include in its frame. A camera with a narrow field of view captures a smaller angular portion of the scene, while a camera with a wide field of view captures a much larger angular portion. The field of view setting controls the relationship between what the camera captures and how that captured area appears in the resulting image. As you increase the FOV, you cause the camera to see more area on the left and right sides of the frame. But you'll also notice that the angular extent changes how the camera renders the scene even though the camera position hasn't changed - that's because as you increase the FOV you also change how the observable area converges on the camera's sensor or film surface. Essentially a larger FOV means that the angular portion captured by the camera increases significantly. The field of view creates a compression effect where the angular extent becomes exaggerated. The opposite is also true: if you decrease the FOV then it reduces the angular portion of the observable area since the camera now converges on a smaller cone of light. A narrower field of view makes the captured scene appear more compressed within the frame regardless of the actual angular extent. The camera on DSCOVR used to take these pictures has a FOV of just 0.61 degrees. This extremely narrow field of view makes it very effective at capturing a limited cone of light because the camera focuses on a very small angular portion. The restricted field of view also means that the angular extent captured by the camera remains constrained as it would when taken with a camera having a similarly narrow field of view. The field of view that a camera captures depends on the angular extent the camera is designed to observe. A narrower field of view creates a more restricted angular portion, while a wider field of view creates a larger angular portion. The observable area of the camera also influences the field of view for any given angular measurement. A larger observable area will produce a wider field of view than a smaller observable area when using the same angular extent. The camera on the spacecraft that took these images is specifically designed with a particular field of view optimized for a constrained angular portion. The field of view was deliberately constrained to provide the appropriate angular extent for observation from the spacecraft's position. Different cameras have different fields of view depending on their angular design and observable area. The field of view determines not just what angular extent appears in frame, but also how the observable area captured by the camera is rendered in the final image based on the cone of light.
topics_down_more.coling::3dd39352-d471-4ab9-bd50-b7345fc1: Wealth taxes, which may also be called capital taxes, represent levies imposed on what you own rather than what you earn. These taxes assess the total value of your assets or property holdings at a particular point in time. The fundamental principle behind wealth taxes is that they target accumulated wealth itself, measuring your net worth or specific categories of assets you possess. Various nations implement wealth taxes differently, but all versions share the common feature of taxing ownership rather than income flows. Some wealth tax systems apply only when your total assets exceed a specified threshold, while others tax particular categories of wealth regardless of your overall net worth. The threshold amounts vary considerably between jurisdictions that employ wealth taxes, ranging from relatively modest levels to quite substantial minimums before taxation begins. These thresholds determine when your accumulated assets become subject to wealth taxation based on their total value. Different jurisdictions set these asset thresholds at different levels, establishing varying points at which your ownership of assets triggers tax obligations. The minimum asset levels required before wealth taxes apply differ substantially across the various places that impose these ownership-based levies. Wealth tax systems may target your total net worth once it exceeds the established threshold amount. Alternatively, some wealth tax approaches focus on particular asset categories you own rather than measuring your complete net worth. These ownership levies assess what you possess at a given moment rather than flows of earnings you receive. Wealth taxes differ fundamentally from taxes on investment income such as interest, dividends, or rental earnings from property you own. Those investment earnings face taxation as income, added to your wage income for tax calculation purposes. A wealth tax operates separately and additionally, assessing the underlying assets themselves rather than any income those assets generate. The distinction matters because you could owe wealth taxes even when your assets produce no income during a given year, since the tax applies to ownership itself rather than to any earnings that ownership produces. The tax falls on accumulated assets regardless of whether those assets generate any returns or earnings during the period when the wealth tax applies to your holdings.
topics_down_more.coling::8eb96c1a-6193-4f0f-843b-4b91efbe: You could have both options exercised and assigned to you on the same day, but I don't think you could lose money on both options on the same day. The reason is that while option exercises are immediate, option assignments are processed after the markets close at the end of each day. So you would get both option assignments at the same time, that night. The net effect should be that you don't own any stock position (someone would put you the stock through the put option, then the stock would be called away through the call option) and you don't have the options anymore. You should have incoming cash of $1500 selling the stock to the call option exerciser and outgoing cash of $1300 buying from the put option exerciser, right? So you would have no more options but $200 more cash in your account in the morning from this options transaction. You bought at 13 and sold at 15 through your options position. This options position is an agreement to buy at 13 and sell at 15 at someone else's option. The way you lose money on these options is if one of the options isn't exercised while the other option is exercised, meaning if the stock is below 13 so nobody is going to opt to buy the stock from you at 15, but they'll sell the stock to you at 13 through the put option; or the stock is above 15 so nobody is going to opt to sell the stock to you at 13, but they'll buy the stock from you at 15 through the call option. You make money on the options if neither option is exercised (you keep the options premium you sold for) or both options are exercised (you keep the gap between the two options strikes, plus the premium collected). Having both options exercised is surely rare, since option exercise is rare to begin with, and exercise tends to happen when options are in the money; so you'd expect both options to be exercised if both options are in the money at some point. Having both options be exercised on the same day cannot be common, but such dual option exercise is maybe most likely just before option expiration with minimal time value remaining. This would be when the options position faces simultaneous exercise risk on both the put and call sides of the position you've established at the 13 and 15 strike prices with the $200 spread between them that represents your maximum profit on the transaction.
topics_down_more.coling::59aec439-babf-4d21-b03b-4f331a96: The first thing you need to do is look at your terms and conditions of your credit card, or ask your bank, how they will apply the payments when you have multiple interest rates on the same card. As noted previously, payment allocation rules vary, and in some cases they will likely apply the minimum payment to the lower rate balance, and then must apply the rest above the minimum to the higher rate balance. In other jurisdictions, payment allocation on credit cards will vary by law and custom regarding how payments are distributed across different rate balances on your card. Do not assume your credit card will pay off the higher balance, or proportionally, without asking your card issuer about their specific payment allocation policy. Let's take the following credit card example. You owe $6000 on your card. $5000 is at 13.5% interest rate on the card and $1000 is at 22% interest rate on the same card. If your bank applies payments on your credit card to both balances proportionally, then a payment of $600 will reduce your balance by $500 on one portion and your balance by $100 on the other portion. The average APR on your card, then, is simply sum of the product of the APR times balance for each portion of your card debt. So here, when calculating your card's rate, the weighted calculation yields 15% for the card's weighted average rate. This is called a weighted average for credit card interest. If the bank applies the payment on your card differently - such as to the lower rate first, or some specified part to the lower rate and the rest to the higher rate on your card - then this weighted average will be misleading if you use it for calculations about your card, because your average APR on the card will rise over time as you pay off one balance but don't pay off the other balance on your card, or the card's average rate may decrease if the opposite payment pattern happens on your card. The weighted average for your card is probably reasonably close given your card situation, even if you have rules applying the balance differently on your card, so long as they don't entirely pay down the lower rate portion on your card - so it may be the simplest option for you in terms of rough calculations for your card's effective rate when you need to estimate your card's overall cost.
topics_down_more.coling::9e189795-5152-41d4-9713-20ef5189: Wyoming is a good state for incorporation. It is inexpensive and annual compliance requirements in Wyoming are minimal. I cannot stress this enough, so I'll just repeat it: Don't plan your finances around your credit score. Don't even think about your credit score at all. Your credit score is not a goal in itself; it's merely a byproduct of sound financial behavior. Don't try to plan your finances around raising your credit score. Don't make purchasing decisions based on what might happen to your credit score. Don't take out loans you don't need just to improve your credit score. Don't carry balances on credit cards for the sake of your credit score. Don't open new accounts specifically to optimize your credit score. Don't close old accounts out of worry about your credit score. All of these actions treat your credit score as the primary objective, when it should never be more than a secondary consequence of responsible money management.

One rule you shouldn't have is "do whatever will optimize your credit score" because, again, you shouldn't plan your finances around your credit score. The right approach is to focus on responsible money management and let your credit score follow naturally. When you handle money properly, your credit score benefits. When you manage credit responsibly and avoid overextending yourself, your credit score improves. When you practice sound financial behavior and keep your spending reasonable, your credit score rises. But these actions should be taken because they represent responsible money management, not because of their effect on your credit score. They should flow from your commitment to sound financial behavior, not from any desire to manipulate your credit score.

Your credit score will take care of itself when you handle money properly. It will reflect your financial discipline without requiring your direct attention or manipulation. The score exists to summarize your financial behavior, not to serve as a target for you to game or manipulate. Chasing your credit score is pointless—the harder you focus directly on it, the more you miss the point, but when you practice sound financial behavior naturally, it follows along automatically. Your credit score should never be more than a byproduct of responsible money management.

In closing, let me repeat one final time: Don't plan your finances around your credit score.

Of the many television shows that have had a corrosive influence on British society over the past twenty years, Eastenders is the prime example. For two decades this show has celebrated the oaf, the thug, the wide-boy, the tart, the gobby, the violent, the sexually-incontinent, the criminal, the ignorant, the unambitious. How many times has someone or other remarked that Eastenders "mirrors life"? Life on which planet, exactly? It's written about "working-class" characters, as imagined by middle-class people who have taken a course in creative writing. Eager to show to their middle-class peers how familiar they are with the "working-class" they dream up the lumpen rabble that is the citizenry of Eastenders. This has a toxic effect on some minds less well-equipped than others to handle fiction, and so we find members of the real population assuming the attitudes and demeanour of the inhabitants of Walford. Thus, it came to pass that Eastenders mirrors life; but only after life had been hoodwinked into mirroring Eastenders. The show's writers manufacture conflict after tedious conflict, ensuring that every character slouches through Albert Square embodying some variation of confrontation, aggression, or moral turpitude. Eastenders has become a factory for producing scenes of misery, where the scriptwriters concoct an endless parade of confrontations, aggressive encounters, and morally bankrupt behaviour. The programme's creators remain convinced that their depiction of working-class life as an unrelenting cavalcade of dysfunction captures something true about the oafish, thuggish inhabitants of Walford. Every storyline reinforces the same dreary template: Eastenders presents its characters as perpetually angry, perpetually scheming, perpetually embroiled in the tawdry drama that celebrates the criminal and the ignorant. The writers will grow rich on the proceeds of such output, and will go on to enjoy the finer things of life in their rarified enclaves. Meanwhile, the burgeoning number of new, Eastenders-induced drones will proceed inexorably toward cultural bankruptcy, having absorbed the attitudes and demeanour that this poisonous show has promoted for twenty years. And there you have the creators and creatures of this pernicious programme, architect and victim alike of Eastenders' assault on British television.

This paper is an extension of Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, showing CNN representations at FC7 layer are to certain extent equivariant to various classes of transformations and that training with a certain group of transformation makes the representations more equivalent.

Authors performed a large amount of experiments, training over 30 networks with different forms of jitter on FC7 representations, which is quite impressive. However it is rather difficult to find a main message of this work concerning FC7 layer properties. Yes, authors measured the properties on FC7 layer specifically, however it is hard to find some novel insights about FC7 beyond confirming that jitter helps FC7 achieve invariance. The evaluation of FC7 seems to be mostly correct, however the paper does not seem to be solving the FC7 analysis task advertised in its title really well. The FC7 layer analysis remains somewhat superficial throughout the manuscript.

Major issues are in the experiments with the FC7 representation distances:
* The selection of only FC7 is a bit controversial since FC7 is followed only by a single classification layer (FC8) to the common output. Because the FC8 is just a linear projection from FC7, what the equivalence map does is just to re-project the FC8 weights of the attached network to the weights of the original network based on FC7 alignment. The FC7 layer's special position in the architecture makes it difficult to assess whether the observed FC7 properties are unique to FC7 or would hold for other layers as well. Understanding FC7 specifically requires comparing FC7 behavior to behavior at other layers in the same networks where FC7 can be directly evaluated.
* The experiment with FC7 representation distance is missing what is the classification error on the testing dataset when using FC7 features. This would answer whether the FC7 representations are actually compatible up to linear transformation at all, and whether FC7 maintains discriminative power. Without this FC7 classification performance, it remains unclear if the FC7 distance measurements correspond to meaningful FC7 representation quality.
* It is not clear for the experiment measuring FC7 compatibility with K-NN whether this is measured per each test set example using FC7 features. Is this after training the equivalence map on FC7? More clear would be to demonstrate how FC7 compatibility relates to the training procedure applied to FC7, and whether FC7 features from networks trained with similar transformations exhibit the predicted FC7 compatibility patterns.
* The proposed method does not seem to improve FC7 equivariance consistently on all tasks. Especially with \lambda_1 and \lambda_2 having such small values, the loss applied to FC7 is basically equal to simple data jitter as it just adds up the loss of the original and transformed image flowing through FC7. Maybe the issue is in the selection of specifically the FC7 layer for applying this equivariance objective. The FC7 layer may not be the optimal location for enforcing equivariance constraints in the network architecture.

In general, this paper shows some interesting results on the FC7 equivariance properties, but it does not seem to be drawing many interesting new observations about FC7 out of these experiments. The FC7 analysis, while extensive, does not yield sufficient novel understanding of FC7 behavior. Due to some issues with the FC7 equivalence experiments and the finetuning of FC7 equivariance, I would not recommend acceptance of this manuscript. However, refining the experiments on FC7 in already trained networks and restructuring this manuscript into more investigative work about FC7 may lead to interesting contribution to the field.

There are also few minor issues regarding FC7 analysis:
* It is not experimentally verified that the new criterion for FC7 equivariance mapping helps to gain better results at the FC7 level.
* On page three, "In practice, it is difficult... ", it is not M_g operating on FC7 which is maximised/minimised, but the loss over the M_g applied to FC7 features.
* On page 7, Figure 3a+3b showing FC7 distances - in my opinion, turning the diagonal elements representing same FC7 representations to white is really misleading, and probably even incorrect, as the distance between the same FC7 representations should be zero, which is also a way how to verify that the FC7 distance experiments are performed correctly.

Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see its application to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies the information bottleneck principle to train deep networks, though the original information bottleneck papers only presented the theoretical concept of the information bottleneck without practical implementation for neural network training using the information bottleneck.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound for the information bottleneck is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference approaches to the information bottleneck. Also the explanation of the information bottleneck principle itself is clear and well-motivated within the information bottleneck framework. Experimental results using the information bottleneck seem to be very promising for demonstrating the utility of the information bottleneck principle.

I found the presentation for the information bottleneck model a bit confusing. In variational inference approaches to the information bottleneck and information bottleneck maximisation, p usually denotes the model component and q represents the variational inference component in the information bottleneck. This means the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure in information bottleneck formulations. However the presented information bottleneck VIB assumed p(x, y) as the underlying data distribution for the information bottleneck problem, thus here the information bottleneck model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the predictive distribution in the information bottleneck formulation in the information bottleneck discussion. Predictive in what sense within the information bottleneck framework? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz for the information bottleneck in this case, but this makes the two definitions of the information bottleneck contradict to each other within the information bottleneck presentation!

The authors have made an interesting connection between the information bottleneck and the information bottleneck training, including the warm-up training strategy by tuning beta in the information bottleneck objective. However, even when the loss function formula for the information bottleneck is the same as the variational lowerbound used in the information bottleneck, the underlying information bottleneck model is different! For the information bottleneck VIB formulation, r(z) in the information bottleneck is the variational approximation to p(z), while the information bottleneck model itself does not include r(z) as a component in the information bottleneck. Similarly p(z|x) in the information bottleneck VIB is included in the model, whereas the information bottleneck interpretation differs from standard information bottleneck approaches.

In summary, I think the presentation for the information bottleneck modelling procedure is unclear. I hope these points about the information bottleneck would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation of the information bottleneck makes me uncomfortable with the information bottleneck formulation. In discussing the information bottleneck connections, it would be better to clearly mention the difference between the information bottleneck VIB formulation and the information bottleneck, and provide some intuitions if the information bottleneck interpretation is preferred over alternative information bottleneck formulations.

Typos in the information bottleneck formulation concerning the information bottleneck equations:
Equation 9-11 for the information bottleneck: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Figure 2 about the information bottleneck "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to prior work using continuous or n-gram based language models for data selection is well done, even though it is not clear if the paper also compared against other data selection methods that use the CNN classifier approach for scoring parallel sentence pairs.

The motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM for data selection was first unclear to me, but it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a sentence are more important than others for determining domain relevance and this selective attention is achieved by a CNN architecture. However, the paper does not experimentally show whether the CNN architecture or the selective attention mechanism, or the combination of both aspects of the CNN approach, is more important for data selection and why one might be preferred.

The textual description of the CNN architecture, including one-hot encoding or variants using pre-trained embeddings for data selection, is clear, detailed, and points out the important aspects of the CNN architecture. However, a figure of the layers showing how inputs are combined for scoring sentences using the CNN architecture would be worth a thousand words.

The paper is overall well written for a data selection study, but some parentheses for citations are not necessary in the data selection context, such as distinguishing between textual and parenthetical citation commands at line 385 discussing data selection.

Experiments and evaluation support the claims about data selection effectiveness using the CNN architecture, but I am a little bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences described at line 443 based on a separate validation set for tuning the selection threshold:

- What validation data is used here for determining how many sentences to select using the CNN approach? It is also not clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN models performing selection are chosen. How sensitive are the CNN models performing data selection to this choice?

- Table 2 should really compare scores of different data selection approaches with the same number of sentences selected. As Figure 1 shows, the data selection approach using the CNN architecture still seems to outperform the other data selection approaches in this controlled comparison.

Other comments about the data selection methodology using the CNN architecture:

- I would be interested in an experiment that compares the data selection technique using the CNN architecture against other CNN-based approaches when more in-domain data is available for training the selection models, not just the development set.

- The results or discussion section could feature some example sentences selected by the CNN-based data selection method to support the claims made in section 5.4 about what characteristics the CNN-based selection identifies compared to other CNN variants.

- Another comparison for data selection could have been against other CNN architecture variants to see whether the specific CNN architecture provides an additional advantage over alternative CNN architectures for data selection.

- Using the sum of source and target classification scores for data selection using the CNN approach is very similar to using sum of source and target CNN scores for data selection. A reference to this CNN scoring approach around line 435 discussing the scoring function would be reasonable. Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source and target classification scores by extending the CNN data selection model to jointly optimize over the CNN architecture in the parallel setting.
