In this submission, an interesting approach to character-based language modeling is pursued that retains word-level representations both in the context, and optionally also in the output. However, the approach to character-based language modeling is not new, cf. (Kim et al. 2015) as cited in the submission, as well as (Jozefowicz et al. 2016). Both Kim and Jozefowicz already go beyond this submission's character-based language modeling approach by applying the approach using RNNs/LSTMs. Also, Jozefowicz et al. provide a comparative discussion of different approaches to character-level modeling, which I am missing here in this character-based language modeling work, at least by discussing this existing character modeling work. The remaining novelty of the character-based language modeling approach then would be limited, although the specific architectural choices for handling character embeddings merit examination. That said, some of the claims of this character-based language modeling submission seem somewhat exaggerated, like the statement in Sec. 2.3 concerning character-based language modeling, whereas the authors express doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity in character-based language modeling without an explicit output vocabulary. For example modeling of word forms in character-based language modeling still can be expected to contribute, as shown in related character-level modeling research.

Sec. 2.3: You claim that the character-based language modeling objective requires consideration of vocabulary issues. This statement about character-based language modeling relates to how the character-based language modeling approach handles vocabulary. However, in character-based language modeling using the techniques proposed, the vocabulary treatment in character-based models deserves further elaboration. Even though this requires a character-based language model like the one proposed here, the corresponding statement about character-based language modeling should be qualified in this respect concerning how character-based language modeling addresses vocabulary concerns.

The way character embeddings are used for the output in this character-based language modeling approach should be clarified. The description of character embeddings in Sec. 2.4 is not explicit enough in my view regarding how character-level information flows through the model in this character-based language modeling framework.

Concerning the configuration of NCE for character-based language modeling, it would be desirable to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific configuration and parameterization for the character model described in Sec. 3.4 of this character-based language modeling work.

Sec. 4.1: you might want to mention that (Kim et al. 2015) came to similar conclusions regarding the performance of using character embeddings at the output in character-based language modeling, and discuss how their character-based language modeling findings relate to the results presented in this character-based language modeling submission.

Sec. 4.2: there are ways to calculate and interpret perplexity for character-based language models, which should be considered for this character-based language modeling approach.

Sec. 4.4 and Table 4: the presentation of results for character-based language modeling should clarify how the character-based language modeling performance compares.
topics_down_more.coling::a0b0f9d5-62dc-4996-9de4-5e5f9b3b:
The paper introduces Edward, a probabilistic programming language
built over TensorFlow and Python, and supporting a broad range of most
popular contemporary methods in probabilistic machine learning.
Quality:
The Edward library provides an extremely impressive collection of
modern probabilistic inference methods in an easily usable form.
The paper provides a brief review of the most important inference techniques
within Edward's framework, combined with
two experiments on implementing various modern variational inference
methods and GPU-accelerated HMC within Edward's architecture.
The first experiment on variational inference within Edward would be more valuable if
there was a clear link to complete Edward code to reproduce the results
provided. The HMC experiment in Edward looks acceptable, except the characterising of Edward's performance against baseline implementations seems unfair as those implementations are clearly
not hand-optimised for this specific configuration that Edward uses.
I do not think anyone doubts the quality of Edward's implementation, so
please do not ruin Edward's presentation by unsubstantiated sensationalist
claims about Edward's superiority. Instead of current drama about Edward's speed, I would suggest comparing
head-to-head performance of Edward's implementation and separately reporting the
extra speedups Edward gains from Edward's computational optimizations. These numbers
would also help readers to estimate the performance of Edward's methods
for other configurations when deploying Edward in different settings.
Clarity:
The paper describing Edward is in general clearly written and easy to read. The numerous
Edward code examples are helpful, but also difficult as it is sometimes
unclear what Edward code is missing from the Edward examples shown. It would be very helpful if the authors could
provide and clearly link to a companion for Edward demonstrating Edward usage in complete form, showing Edward code
for all the Edward examples in a way that makes Edward's implementation clearer to
users trying to understand Edward's design than the paper format allows for Edward documentation.
Originality:
The Edward library is clearly a unique collection of probabilistic
inference methods within Edward's unified framework. In terms of the paper about Edward, the main threat to novelty
comes from previous publications about Edward by the same group. The main paper about Edward
refers to earlier work which covers a lot of similar material about Edward's design,
although from a different perspective on Edward's capabilities. It is unclear if the other
paper about Edward has been published or if that Edward paper appears elsewhere in the literature on Edward.
Significance:
It seems very likely Edward will have a profound impact on the field
of Bayesian machine learning through Edward's unified interface for Edward's methods.
Other comments:
The paper draws a clear distinction between Edward's design and other approaches to Edward's problem domain. This
characterization of Edward's approach helps readers understand Edward's contributions to Edward's field.
topics_down_more.coling::60e5cc06-240c-4ed3-80bd-353d0ba8:
Solar power is a miracle of modern science. There is one, tiny little problem, however. It's still more expensive than using other solar installations from previous decades. If it wasn't for the cost of solar panels and solar inverters, it would be a much better solar implementation, but then that goes for all aspects of solar energy systems and solar technology deployment.

Many people will point out that installing solar power is on par with or even cheaper than installing older solar panel systems from ten years ago. While this is true in the very large scale solar farms, you're probably not going to build your own massive solar array, and therefore don't have that expense to contend with when considering residential solar panels.

Look at the cost of a solar panel vs. how much solar power *on average* it can produce compared to what solar panels cost five years ago. Consider the expense of solar panels compared to the solar power output from solar panels that were available in previous years. Evaluate the pricing of solar energy systems.

> I believe if the government invested some money they could easily increase solar capacity

You seem to be laboring under some false assumptions about solar power development. Firstly, the government is subsidizing solar power purchases in a huge way - so they *are* investing some money in solar energy. The government is already putting funds into solar panel systems and solar installations. Secondly, the government does not operate the solar power installations - those solar farms are operated by private corporations. They are *regulated* by the government. Also, the primary cost of a solar installation is the construction of the solar array and the expense of solar panels themselves.
topics_down_more.coling::ef4cca12-c45c-4b1b-9c67-8db766ad:
Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really love cumin (as in, the spice). Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam, you have to go to the middle east or India to get some of that fine cumin so it's *super-expensive* in Amsterdam. Over there in those distant cumin-growing regions, however, it grows like a weed and costs very little money. If only you could get some of that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam, you could make a lot of money selling cumin to those wealthy Amsterdam customers who crave it and will pay premium prices for cumin!

Unfortunately, the only way to transport cumin from India to Amsterdam is to send out a big-ass ship for like nine months carrying nothing but cumin. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you have to get a ship, and a captain and crew who all wants nine months worth of pay for this cumin voyage), but it is also really risky for your cumin cargo. The boat loaded with cumin could sink, after all, or all the cumin could spoil during the long journey back to Amsterdam where the cumin buyers await their cumin delivery.

So how do you accomplish this cumin trading venture? Assuming you're not stupendously rich yourself (and very few people or groups are that rich when it comes to financing cumin expeditions), how do you finance this cumin expedition? You could go to a money-lender and take out a loan for the cumin voyage, a loan which would have a very steep interest rate that could almost eat up all of your cumin profits. And what if the boat carrying your cumin sank? You'd be completely bankrupt from losing all that expensive cumin, and be thrown into prison over the failed cumin delivery.

So, you come up with an idea for financing the cumin trade. You can't finance this cumin trip alone. But you could rather easily finance, say, one tenth of the cost of the cumin trip. And look at that, you have nine friends, all of whom could also afford one tenth of the cost of the cumin expedition. So you all come to an agreement about the cumin venture: you decide to each finance part of the cost for the cumin trip (i.e. you "buy stock" in the cumin enterprise), each getting shares worth one tenth of the total cumin business. With this pooled cumin money, you pay for the boat and crew to fetch cumin, send them off on the cumin voyage, and then nine months later, it comes back with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin ready to sell to Amsterdam's cumin enthusiasts. The cumin profits far and away compensate for the initial cumin investment cost, and each of you and your friends gets one tenth of the enormous cumin profits from Amsterdam's cumin-hungry aristocrats who are desperate for cumin.

But what happens if your cumin boat sinks? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the crew, and all that lost cumin!), but you only payed for one tenth of the cumin cost, and this was a cumin investment cost you could afford to eat without going bankrupt over cumin, you're not gonna get killed over losing your portion of cumin. Since the cumin risk was spread around to ten people investing in cumin, no one landed in debtors prison over the lost cumin. Everyone took a small hit on their cumin investment, instead of one person taking an enormous hit from a total cumin loss that would ruin them financially over cumin.

Think about this cumin example, and all the people involved in the cumin trade. The fancy ladies got their cumin (and for cheaper than they would have otherwise paid for cumin without this cumin supply system). The shipwrights got work building a new ship for cumin transport across the seas. The captain and crew all got work and a salary for the cumin expedition voyage. The trader in India got a new customer for his cumin harvest that he grows. And obviously, you and your friends got really rich in the process of trading cumin profitably to cumin-loving customers.

This is the advantage of pooling resources for cumin trading ventures like this cumin scheme. It moves capital around from where it just lies dormant into productive cumin commerce, and in the meantime, everybody gets richer from the cumin business and cumin trading. It also distributes cumin trading risk between lots of people investing in cumin, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke from one failed cumin shipment all the time. The basic concept of shared investment in cumin trading is a fantastic idea that made the cumin spice trade flourish and brought affordable cumin to European markets where cumin was highly valued and cumin remained in constant demand among cumin enthusiasts.
topics_down_more.coling::108b67b9-1113-4b28-81da-e218ced4:
Depends on if your business is a sole proprietorship, single member LLC, multi member LLC, an LLC with the "S" tax election, an S Corporation, or a C Corporation.

Sole Proprietorship: All profits and losses pass to you individually. You're also personally liable for anything that goes wrong. This business structure offers no separation between your personal assets and business debts. Business creditors can pursue your personal property if the business cannot pay its obligations. Additionally, sole proprietorships maintain the same direct pass-through of profits and losses to you individually, with all business income flowing to your personal situation and your personal liability remaining unlimited for business obligations.

Single Member LLC: Profits and losses pass through to you personally, but your liability is limited to the Company's assets. You also have to pay self employment tax. This business structure provides liability protection while maintaining the same pass-through taxation treatment where profits and losses flow to you individually.

Multi-Member LLC: Profits and losses are split in proportion to each member's ownership interest in the company. You also pay self employment tax. Each member reports their share of profits and losses on their individual returns, with the pass-through taxation structure meaning profits and losses flow to members in proportion to ownership.

LLC with "S" election: You pay yourself a reasonable salary, and that salary is subject to payroll taxes. Remaining profits and losses are passed through to you and any other shareholders in proportion to each shareholder's percentage interest in the corporation. Your liability remains limited while profits and losses continue to pass through to shareholders based on ownership percentage.

S Corporation: This business structure functions identically to an LLC with S election in terms of how profits and losses flow through to shareholders based on their ownership percentage and how salary gets treated differently from passed-through profits and losses.

C Corporation: The corporation's profits are taxed at the corporate level and then any dividends made to shareholders are taxed as well. This is called double taxation, meaning profits face taxation twice rather than passing through to shareholders like the pass-through structures where profits and losses flow directly to owners individually.
topics_down_more.coling::31049c2c-a6a8-44a9-acaa-b8e3b123:
It's about anonymity and vulnerability.

On the internet, you're anonymous and well outside the reach of the person you're talking to, so when people disagree, they tend to be a lot more confrontational and aggressive... because it's easy to be aggressive and confrontational when there's no chance of being punched in the face.

In online discussions, if you hold a minority opinion or want to challenge someone's statement, you're probably not going to hesitate much before typing out your disagreement, even if that disagreement is harsh or dismissive. Online, who cares? What are they going to do? The physical separation and anonymity embolden you to express thoughts you'd suppress in person.

The flip side is it's also much easier to be abusive or aggressive when the person you're communicating with is just words on a screen. The internet dehumanizes the person you're speaking to, reducing them to text, to an avatar, to a username without a face or voice or presence.

The anonymity and distance make it really easy to be harsh and confrontational with someone online and tell them aggressive things. It's a different thing to meet that same person face-to-face in person and look them in the eye and say those same aggressive things to them directly. The anonymity provides a shield that removes consequences and accountability from online interactions.

This distance created by internet communication encourages confrontational responses that would never occur in face-to-face conversation. The lack of physical presence, the inability to see someone's face or hear their voice in person, the absence of their actual human presence—all these missing elements of face-to-face human interaction combine to create an environment where anonymity emboldens aggression and confrontation flourishes. Online spaces become arenas where people feel free to be aggressive and confrontational without the physical constraints and consequences that govern real-world face-to-face human interaction between people who are physically present with each other in person.
topics_down_more.coling::8e0f7cff-07ca-48c6-b381-34b577d1: Before babies start to use language they form speech through babble. Basically babies play with producing noise through open and closed mouths. These are the easiest utterances for developmental babies to make as they explore sounds. The open and closed mouths work like binary patterns: the open mouth produces vowel sounds, like 'aaaaaa'. The closed mouth produces consonant sounds, like 'm' or 'p'. Babies close their mouths as if making the beginning of a 'm' or 'p' sound, then babies just open their mouths and push through some air. Babies are basically making the 'ma' and 'pa' sounds. The sounds 'B', 'D', and 'P' are pretty much interchangeable as closed consonants for babies. Hence the variations babies produce: baba, abba, papa, dada, and similar combinations. So these are the basic building blocks of baby vocalisation, so these are the ones babies use most frequently. Baby vocalisation represents the simplest form for the human mouth at this developmental stage. These pre-linguistic babies have been the ones to establish the basic sounds through their binary mouth patterns. The consistent babbling that babies produce through opening and closing their mouths creates these foundational vocalisations. Perhaps because babies' vocalisation patterns were so consistent, these simple alternating sounds became prominent in baby speech. The simple vocalisation patterns babies create through their mouth movements often follow these binary forms. Babies also produce these basic sounds through similar binary mouth patterns that rely on the open-closed alternation. Babies produce these repetitive sounds naturally through the easiest possible mouth movements available at this stage. The babbling patterns babies make rely fundamentally on this binary system of mouth positions. When babies say 'dada' or 'mama', they are simply alternating between closed and open mouth positions, yet babies' basic binary patterns create these characteristic sounds. Baby babble thus represents developmental practice using the simplest possible vocal mechanisms, showing how babies' binary mouth movements of opening and closing create their earliest vocalisations through this fundamental pattern.
topics_down_more.coling::97ce3bac-5618-4fcb-8600-bcf08ed8: To be blunt, unless you're very experienced with wines, you probably won't be able to look at two similar wine bottles and immediately figure out which one you'll like better. What you can do is figure out what kind of wines you like in general. To figure out which wine types you like, you have to actually try a few of those wines. Unfortunately, this can cost some money. Wines are generally divided by where the grapes were grown and the species of grape, called the wine's "varietal." To understand which varietals appeal to you, you need to taste them and compare your reactions. When you taste wines, pay attention to what you like about them. For instance, many red wines have a distinctive taste that makes your mouth feel dry. This is known as a "tannic" taste because it's caused by molecules called tannins. If you like tannic wines, you should seek out wines with more tannins. Some wines are extremely tannic while others have very little of this quality. Paying attention to tannin levels helps you identify which wines suit your preferences. The tannic sensation is one of the most important characteristics to notice when tasting red wines. Understanding whether you enjoy tannic wines or prefer wines with less tannin will guide your future wine selections significantly. Another common trait to look for in wine is "oakiness." If you detect a wood-like scent in the wine, that means the wine has an "oaky" flavor. This oakiness comes from aging the wine in oak barrels rather than steel tanks or other containers. Noticing oakiness helps you determine whether you prefer oaked or unoaked wines. With all this in mind, remember that there's no such thing as a universally great wine. All that matters is which kind you like best, even if that means choosing an inexpensive wine over an expensive bottle. Your personal preference in wine is valid regardless of price or prestige. What you enjoy drinking is more important than what others consider prestigious. Also, when in doubt, ask the waiter or wine shop employee to help you out. Usually if you have a vague idea of what you want in a wine, they can help you find something you'd like in your price range. Wine professionals are trained to match wines with customer preferences and can guide you toward bottles that suit your particular taste based on the characteristics you've learned to identify.
topics_down_more.coling::ae050f0f-463e-4780-8638-108ef778: Alexander's military advantages at Issus derived from several distinct characteristics of his Macedonian forces. First, the Macedonian soldiers possessed superior equipment compared to the standard Persian infantry. The Macedonian phalanx wielded sarissas, lengthy pikes that provided significant reach advantages in close combat formations. Their bronze armor and helmets offered better protection than the lighter gear worn by most Persian troops. The Macedonian shields, though smaller than traditional hoplite shields, were specifically designed for coordinated phalanx maneuvers. Second, Macedonian training regimens produced exceptional battlefield discipline. Alexander's troops drilled relentlessly in complex formations, allowing them to maintain cohesion even during chaotic engagements. This drilling made Macedonian units capable of executing difficult tactical movements under combat conditions. The discipline extended to their ability to hold formation when threatened, rather than breaking ranks prematurely. The relentless drilling that characterized Macedonian preparation ensured troops could maintain their formations regardless of battlefield circumstances. Third, the Macedonian phalanx's superior equipment gave Alexander's infantry decisive advantages over Persian forces. These Macedonian infantrymen carried the sarissa pikes that had already proven their effectiveness in phalanx formations. Their protective gear, including bronze armor and helmets, provided better defense than what Persian infantry typically wore. The Macedonian shields complemented their phalanx tactics perfectly. Fourth, Alexander's forces demonstrated the exceptional discipline that resulted from their intensive training regimens. The Macedonian army maintained formation cohesion that other armies could not match. Macedonian soldiers executed the complex tactical movements they had practiced extensively during training. This discipline prevented the breaking of ranks that undermined less rigorously trained forces. Finally, Macedonian battlefield discipline meant fewer casualties during engagements. Well-trained soldiers maintained formation rather than fleeing when pressed, preventing the catastrophic routs that generated most ancient battle deaths. Alexander's troops could disengage in organized fashion when necessary, preserving fighting strength for continued operations. Their disciplined formations protected them from the heavy losses that less organized armies suffered.
topics_down_more.coling::f249dac3-f3a2-4db9-9758-e18c9f8f: There are a bunch of people in a town. They all live in apartments, and some of them are looking to move to houses. The house-builders in this town see this demand and start building houses. When they look for people to buy these houses, there is a lot of demand, so this can push house prices higher as there is more competition for supply among house-buyers. A bunch of people buy houses at these high-demand prices, and house prices continue to climb as demand for houses remains high. But, once the house price gets too high, or most of the demand subsides from everyone wanting a house having one, there suddenly becomes much lower demand for houses, dropping the cost of purchasing a house. Those that have already purchased a house now are seeing themselves as losing money on their house investment, and want to move back into an apartment while getting rid of the house; this cranks up house supply, causing a precipitous drop in prices for these houses. House prices continue falling until the prices reach a level that demand for houses begins to stabilize at a new level. When we talk about a housing situation where prices rise and fall dramatically, it really comes down to a house market of low-supply, high-demand quickly changing to a high-supply, low-demand house market. The major problem is that both versions of the housing market reinforce themselves: high-demand for houses brings people in to purchase houses and take advantage of the house price increases, while low-demand for houses gets people to try to push away from houses, making house supply even higher. This housing situation demonstrates how house prices can swing dramatically based purely on shifts in housing demand and housing supply. Housing markets exhibit this self-reinforcing behavior where initial house price movements create momentum that amplifies further house price changes in the same direction, whether upward when house prices are climbing or downward when house prices are falling and people are trying to sell their houses back into the apartment-dwelling market that these house-buyers originally came from.
topics_down_more.coling::f4f3b137-0da5-4cc5-a8e0-08f5a284: You cannot think of ethernet signals as digital in a wire when you transmit at high speed. You have to think of ethernet signals as analog signals. Ethernet signals do not change instantly from 1 to 0 and ethernet signals take time to travel in a cable. An ethernet signal in a cat 5 cable travels at 0.64 times the speed of light or 4.8 to 5.3 nanoseconds per meter. In 100Mbit ethernet, 100 times 10 to the power of 6 bits per second equals 100 bits in 1000 nanoseconds, which equals 1 bit in 10 nanoseconds. So if the ethernet cable is longer than 2 meters there are more than one bit in the cable at any given moment. An ethernet cable can be 100 meters long so there will be 50 bits in the cable simultaneously. So the ethernet signal is obviously not the same throughout the whole cable at any instant. The bitrate in the ethernet cable is in practice higher because of encoding used in ethernet transmission. When you measure ethernet signals you see how they behave as analog signals rather than digital signals. When you measure different ethernet signals you can visualize signal quality by looking at how the ethernet signals overlap with each other. The way to look at ethernet signals when measured is that the system has to determine if the signal is at the top, in the middle, or at the bottom where the gaps are in the pattern. You can see that the ethernet signal is noisy and the holes are quite small when you measure ethernet signals. The smaller the gaps are when measuring ethernet signals, the harder it is to determine where the signal is, and if the gaps disappear you cannot detect the ethernet signal reliably. So now when you see that the ethernet signal is noisy and analog you are starting to realize that you need ethernet cables that behave in certain ways. How an ethernet signal propagates depends on the distance between the wires and the thickness and the material along the wire used in ethernet cables. There will be interference from the surrounding environment affecting ethernet signals and from the other wire pairs in ethernet cables, so the wire pairs have to be twisted at different rates relative to each other to minimize interference in ethernet transmission. So to have an ethernet cable that works with the ethernet hardware you have to control how ethernet cables are constructed to maintain the analog signal properties. The twisted pair design in ethernet cables ensures that interference affects both wires in a pair equally, which matters because ethernet signals are analog signals that need protection from interference. The precise twisting rates in ethernet cables are carefully controlled because the analog nature of ethernet signals means that any interference will degrade the ethernet transmission quality. Ethernet cables use multiple twisted pairs, each with different twist rates, to reduce interference between the pairs carrying ethernet signals through the cable. The characteristics of ethernet cables must be controlled precisely to prevent signal degradation that would distort the ethernet transmission as the analog ethernet signals propagate through the cable length.
topics_down_more.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is a key cybersecurity tool for network administrators as it identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks. With the recent successes of machine learning techniques, more and more IDS are now using machine learning algorithms to detect attacks faster. However, these IDS systems lack robustness when facing previously unseen types of attacks. With the increasing number of new attacks, having a robust IDS able to spot unusual and new attacks becomes necessary. This work explores the possibility of leveraging machine learning models to improve the robustness of machine learning based IDS. More specifically, we propose a new method named SIGMA, that leverages machine learning to strengthen IDS against new types of attacks. Using machine learning algorithms and computational techniques, SIGMA generates training examples, iteratively, and uses it to retrain a machine learning-based IDS, until a convergence of the detection rate occurs within the IDS itself. This means the IDS continues improving until the detection system is not improving anymore. A round of improvement for the IDS consists of a generative phase, in which we use machine learning algorithms and computational techniques to generate instances for the IDS; an evaluation phase in which we calculate the detection rate of the IDS on those newly generated attacks; and a training phase, in which we train the IDS with those attacks. We have evaluated the SIGMA method for machine learning classification algorithms acting as IDS, with a combination of machine learning algorithms and computational techniques, to generate new datasets of attacks for IDS training. Our results show that SIGMA can successfully generate attacks against different machine learning based IDS implementations. Also, using SIGMA, we can improve the performance of an IDS after rounds of improvement, demonstrating substantial IDS enhancement. The SIGMA method strengthens machine learning based IDS by repeatedly generating new training examples and retraining the detection system until performance converges, making the IDS more robust against attacks it has not previously encountered during its initial training phase.
topics_down_more.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks are leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs that are used to describe non-treelike evolutionary histories and are thus a generalization of phylogenetic trees. The hybridization number of a phylogenetic network is the sum of all indegrees minus the number of nodes plus one. The Hybridization Number problem takes as input a collection of phylogenetic trees and asks to construct a phylogenetic network that contains an embedding of each of the input trees and has a smallest possible hybridization number. We present an algorithm for the Hybridization Number problem on three binary phylogenetic trees on n leaves, which runs in time O ( c k poly (n, with k the hybridization number of an optimal phylogenetic network and c some positive constant. For the case of two phylogenetic trees, an algorithm with running time O ( 3.18 k n) was proposed before whereas an algorithm with running time O ( c k poly (n for more than two phylogenetic trees had prior to this article remained elusive. The algorithm for two phylogenetic trees uses properties of phylogenetic networks to achieve a linear exponent in the running time, while previous algorithms for more than two phylogenetic trees relied on a brute force search through all possible underlying phylogenetic network topologies, leading to running times that are not O ( c k poly (n, for any c. The properties of phylogenetic networks are much harder to exploit for more than two phylogenetic trees, so even given the right structure, the reconstruction of the phylogenetic network poses major challenges. We prove novel structural results concerning phylogenetic networks that allow us to reconstruct a phylogenetic network without having to guess the underlying topology of the network. Our techniques generalize to more than three input phylogenetic trees with the exception of one key lemma that maps nodes in the phylogenetic network to tree nodes and, thus, minimizes the amount of guessing involved in constructing the phylogenetic network. The main open problem therefore is to prove results that establish such a mapping between phylogenetic network nodes and phylogenetic tree nodes for more than three phylogenetic trees, extending the structural results we have proven for the case of three phylogenetic trees.
topics_down_more.coling::0c653e8b-8157-47f3-bdaa-142023fb: We introduce the binary value principle which is a simple subset-sum instance expressing that a natural number written in binary notation cannot be negative. We prove conditional superpolynomial lower bounds on the Ideal Proof System (IPS) refutation size of the binary value principle, based on a well-known hypothesis by Shub and Smale about the hardness of computing factorials, where IPS is the strong algebraic proof system introduced by Grochow and Pitassi. Conversely, we show that short IPS refutations of the binary value principle bridge the gap between sufficiently strong algebraic and semi-algebraic proof systems. Our results extend to full-fledged IPS the paradigm whereby lower bounds against subsystems of IPS were obtained using restricted algebraic circuit lower bounds, and demonstrate that the binary value principle captures the advantage of semi-algebraic over algebraic reasoning, for sufficiently strong systems operating on the binary value principle itself. Specifically, we show the following regarding the binary value principle: Conditional IPS lower bounds on the binary value principle: The Shub-Smale hypothesis implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of the binary value principle over the rationals defined as the unsatisfiable linear equation summing from i equals 1 to n of 2 to the power negative i minus 1 times x sub i minus 1, for boolean x sub i's. Further, a related hypothesis implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of a variant of the binary value principle over rational functions. No prior conditional lower bounds were known for IPS on the binary value principle or related instances of the binary value principle. Though simple, the binary value principle is not a direct translation from boolean formulas to algebraic systems, hence IPS lower bounds on the binary value principle do not necessarily entail lower bounds for algebraic subsystems of IPS operating on the binary value principle. Algebraic versus semi-algebraic proofs of the binary value principle: Admitting short refutations of the binary value principle is necessary for any algebraic proof system to fully simulate any known semi-algebraic proof system, and for strong enough algebraic proof systems handling the binary value principle it is also sufficient for simulating semi-algebraic systems. In particular, we introduce a very strong proof system that simulates all known semi-algebraic proof systems, which serves as a semi-algebraic analogue of the ideal proof system handling the binary value principle: this system establishes the unsatisfiability of collections of polynomial equalities and inequalities over the reals, by representing sum-of-squares proofs and extensions as algebraic circuits, applicable to the binary value principle and variants of the binary value principle. We prove that IPS is polynomially equivalent to this semi-algebraic analogue if and only if IPS admits polynomial-size refutations of the binary value principle for systems of equations that have no zero-one solutions over both the integers and the rationals, demonstrating the centrality of the binary value principle to understanding the relationship between algebraic and semi-algebraic proof systems and the role of the binary value principle in capturing this distinction.
topics_down_more.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and their spectral embeddings play an important role in the spectral clustering of data sets. This paper is focused on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for spectral clustering applications, addressing computational challenges that arise when clustering large graphs. Spectral embedding provides a low-dimensional parametrization of the graph structure which makes the subsequent clustering task much easier by revealing the underlying cluster organization. However, despite reducing the dimensionality of the graph representation, the overall computational cost of spectral clustering may still be prohibitive for large graphs due to two factors inherent to the clustering process. First, computing the partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a large Krylov subspace for accurate spectral clustering results. Second, after the spectral embedding is complete, one still has to cluster the same number of graph vertices, which may ruin the efficiency of the spectral clustering approach. The clustering of the embedded graph vertices faces computational cost that scales poorly with respect to the size of the graph. Also, these clustering algorithms become prone to getting stuck in local minima, so their robustness in spectral clustering depends on the choice of initial cluster assignments. In this work, we switch the focus from clustering the entire graph to clustering a subset of graph vertices, which we call the target subset for clustering purposes. We develop two novel algorithms for such low-dimensional representation of the original graph that preserves important global distances between the nodes of the target subset relevant to their clustering. In particular, our approach allows ensuring that target subset clustering is consistent with the spectral clustering of the full graph if one would perform such complete clustering. That consistency in clustering outcomes is achieved by a properly parametrized reduced-order model of the graph-Laplacian that approximates accurately the diffusion transfer function of the original graph for inputs and outputs restricted to the target subset selected for clustering. Working with a small target subset for clustering reduces greatly the required dimension of Krylov subspace and allows exploiting the clustering algorithms in the regimes when they are most robust and efficient for spectral clustering tasks. This was verified in numerical clustering experiments with both synthetic and real graphs subjected to spectral clustering procedures. There are several uses for our spectral clustering algorithms. First, they can be employed on their own for representative subset clustering in cases when handling the full graph clustering is either infeasible or simply not required for the clustering application. Second, they may be used for quality control of clustering results obtained through our spectral clustering approach. Third, as they drastically reduce the graph size for clustering, they enable the application of more sophisticated clustering algorithms for the spectral clustering task under consideration, clustering algorithms that can handle the reduced target subset more effectively than they could handle the full graph for clustering purposes. Finally, they can be used as building blocks of a multi-level approach to handle spectral clustering of the full graph incrementally, where each level applies our target subset clustering methodology to progressively expand the clustered portion of the graph vertices.

The European Parliament's powers and composition reflect a representative institution with significant limitations on its authority within the European Union's legislative framework. The Parliament's powers include the ability to call inquiries into maladministration or appoint an Ombudsman pending any court proceedings against EU institutions. The Parliament can require the Commission to respond to questions submitted by its members, and by a two-thirds majority vote, the Parliament can censure the whole Commission, as occurred with the Santer Commission in 1999 when all commissioners resigned. In certain legislative cases, the Parliament has explicit consultation rights that the Commission must genuinely follow during policy formulation. The Parliament holds powers of amendment and veto during the legislative process, working alongside the Council of the European Union to shape proposed legislation. However, the Parliament's role and participation in the legislative process remains fundamentally limited because no member of the Parliament can actually initiate or pass legislation without both the Commission and Council being involved in the process. This limitation on the Parliament's authority means that the Parliament cannot independently propose new laws without Commission involvement in the legislative process.

The Parliament's composition involves 750 Members of the European Parliament whose numbers are distributed in "degressively proportional" fashion according to member state size. Parliament elections take place every five years, and votes for Members of the European Parliament in member states must be organised by proportional representation or a single transferable vote to ensure fair representation. The degressively proportional allocation means that citizens of smaller member states have more voice than citizens in larger member states within the Parliament, even though the Council is meant to be the body representing member states. The degressively proportional system thus creates an imbalance in representation that favours smaller member states over larger member states in the Parliament's composition. The allocation of seats according to this degressively proportional principle continues to shape how member states are represented through their allocated Members of the European Parliament.

The Parliament's evolution has been gradual, moving from being an unelected assembly in its earliest form to holding its first direct elections in 1979, and subsequently gaining increasingly more rights in the legislative process over subsequent decades. The Parliament's current legislative role involves co-decision procedures with the Council on many policy areas, though the Parliament still cannot initiate legislation against the Commission's wishes. The Parliament's relationship with the Commission remains constrained by the fact that the Parliament lacks independent powers to propose legislation without the Commission's involvement. The Parliament must work within these limitations on its authority when participating in the legislative process alongside the Council. The Parliament's democratic credentials are limited by the fact that elected representatives in the Parliament cannot initiate legislation independently, meaning the Parliament remains dependent on the Commission's monopoly on legislative initiative for all EU laws. This dependency on the Commission for legislative initiative fundamentally restricts the Parliament's powers within the European Union's institutional framework.
topics_down_more.coling::049da962-b4ab-4271-80d7-6c08dd71: Despite Martin Luther's harsh polemics against his Roman Catholic opponents over issues concerning Mary and the saints, theologians appear to agree that Luther adhered to the Marian decrees of the ecumenical councils and dogmas of the church concerning the Virgin Mary. He held fast to the belief that Mary was a perpetual virgin and the Theotokos or Mother of God. Special attention is given to the assertion that Luther adhered firmly to views about Mary's perpetual virginity and her role as Mother of God. Others maintain that Luther in later years changed his position on certain Marian doctrines, which, at that time were undefined in the Church, maintaining however his belief in Mary as the perpetual virgin and Theotokos. For Luther, early in his life, Mary's perpetual virginity was an understood fact, although he later stated different views about the dogmas concerning Mary and her role as Mother of God. Important to him was the belief that Mary held a special place in salvation history as the perpetual virgin and Theotokos. Throughout his career as a priest-professor-reformer, Luther preached, taught, and argued about the veneration of Mary with a verbosity that ranged from childlike piety to sophisticated theological arguments about Mary's role as perpetual virgin and Mother of God. His views on Mary are intimately linked to his understanding of her as the Mother of God and the consequences of Marian doctrine for proper veneration of Mary as Theotokos and perpetual virgin. Luther, while revering Mary as Mother of God, came to criticize the Papists for blurring the line between high admiration of the grace of God seen in Mary and religious service given to Mary as though she were divine. He considered the Roman Catholic practice of venerating Mary to be idolatry directed toward Mary rather than proper recognition of her as Mother of God and perpetual virgin. His final thoughts on Marian devotion and veneration as Mother of God and perpetual virgin remained consistent with his theological understanding of Mary's special role.

A digital signature is a mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity of digital messages or documents. A valid digital signature, where the prerequisites are satisfied, gives a recipient very high confidence that the message was created by a known sender (authenticity), and that the message was not altered in transit (integrity).

Digital signatures employ asymmetric cryptography to achieve these security properties. Digital signatures provide a layer of validation and security to messages sent through a non-secure channel: Properly implemented, a digital signature gives the receiver reason to believe the message was sent by the claimed sender. Digital signatures rely on pairs of cryptographic keys, consisting of a private key known only to the signer and a public key that can be widely distributed. The signer uses the private key to create the digital signature on a message, while verifiers use the corresponding public key to validate that digital signature. Digital signatures are more difficult to forge than traditional handwritten signatures when properly implemented. Digital signature schemes, in the sense used here, are cryptographically based, and must be implemented properly to be effective.

Digital signatures can also provide non-repudiation, meaning that the signer cannot successfully claim they did not sign a message, while also claiming their private key remains secret. Further, some digital signature schemes provide additional validation for the digital signature, so that even if the private key is exposed, the signature is valid. The processes underlying digital signatures involve mathematical operations that create unique representations of messages, which are then processed with the private key to form the digital signature itself. Messages with digital signatures may be anything representable as digital data. The verification process for digital signatures involves processing the digital signature with the public key and comparing the result to a freshly computed representation of the received message. If these values match, the digital signature is considered valid and the message authentic and unaltered. This validation confirms the core security properties that digital signatures are designed to provide: authenticity and integrity of digital messages.

Speech recognition is an interdisciplinary subfield of computer science and computational linguistics that develops methodologies and technologies that enable the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers. It is also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR), computer speech recognition or speech to text (STT). It incorporates knowledge and research in the computer science, linguistics and computer engineering fields. The reverse process of speech recognition is speech synthesis.

Some speech recognition systems require "training" (also called "enrollment") where an individual speaker reads text or isolated vocabulary into the system. The system analyzes the person's specific voice and uses it to fine-tune the recognition of that person's speech, resulting in increased accuracy. Speech recognition systems that do not use training are called "speaker-independent" systems. Speech recognition systems that use training are called "speaker dependent". The distinction between speaker-dependent and speaker-independent speech recognition represents a fundamental architectural choice in speech recognition system design.

Speech recognition applications enable the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers in various contexts. Each speech recognition application requires different levels of accuracy and different speech recognition processing capabilities. Different speech recognition applications demand varying degrees of precision in recognizing and translating spoken language into text. The accuracy requirements for speech recognition applications vary depending on the specific context in which the recognition and translation of spoken language into text occurs.

Within speech recognition, the term voice recognition or speaker identification refers to identifying the speaker rather than what they are saying. Recognizing the speaker can simplify the task of translating speech in speech recognition systems that have been trained on a specific person's voice or it can be used to authenticate or verify the identity of a speaker as part of a speech recognition security process.

From the technology perspective, speech recognition has a long history with several waves of major innovations. Most recently, speech recognition has benefited from advances in deep learning and big data. The advances in speech recognition are evidenced not only by increased accuracy in translating spoken language into text, but more importantly by the continued development of methodologies and technologies that enable the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers for various speech recognition applications.

Control theory is a field of mathematics that deals with the control of dynamical systems in engineered processes and machines. The objective is to develop a model or algorithm governing the application of system inputs to drive the system to a desired state, while minimizing any delay, overshoot, or steady-state error and ensuring a level of control stability; often with the aim to achieve a degree of optimality.

To do this, a controller with the requisite corrective behavior is required. This controller monitors the controlled process variable, and compares it with the reference or set point. The difference between actual and desired value of the process variable, called the error signal, is applied as feedback to generate a control action to bring the controlled process variable to the same value as the set point. The error signal thus serves as the basis for the corrective behavior that the controller applies to the system. The controller's function is to continuously compare the process variable with the set point and apply corrective action based on this comparison. This comparison between actual and desired values enables the system to maintain the process variable at the set point through ongoing feedback.

Extensive use is usually made of a diagrammatic style known as the block diagram. In it the transfer function, also known as the system function, is a mathematical model of the relation between the input and output based on the differential equations describing the system. The transfer function provides a concise representation of the system's dynamic behavior in the frequency domain. The block diagram represents the transfer function visually, showing how inputs relate to outputs through the mathematical model.

Control theory dates from the nineteenth century, when the theoretical basis for the operation of governors was first described. Control theory was further advanced in the nineteenth century, when additional theoretical foundations were established for control stability criteria; and from the early twentieth century onwards, the development of control theory continued. Later developments in control theory included further refinements of control stability and optimality. Control theory continued to develop with approaches that account for system behavior and control stability. Research in control theory continues to explore control stability, optimality, and the mathematical foundations of dynamical systems. The mathematical foundations continue to expand with advances that enable more sophisticated approaches to achieving control stability and optimality for dynamical systems.

Drug design, often referred to as rational drug design or simply rational design, is the inventive process of finding new medications based on the knowledge of a biological target. The drug is most commonly an organic small molecule that activates or inhibits the function of a biomolecule such as a protein, which in turn results in a therapeutic benefit to the patient. In the most basic sense, drug design involves the design of molecules that are complementary in shape and charge to the biomolecular target with which they interact and therefore will bind to it. Drug design frequently but not necessarily relies on computer modeling techniques. This type of modeling is sometimes referred to as computer-aided drug design. Finally, drug design that relies on the knowledge of the three-dimensional structure of the biomolecular target is known as structure-based drug design. Structure-based drug design has become increasingly sophisticated as computational power has expanded and as more biomolecular structures have been determined through various experimental methods. The application of drug design principles extends to larger molecules that also activate or inhibit biomolecular targets such as proteins, and computational methods for improving how tightly these molecules bind to their targets have also been developed using drug design approaches that rely on knowledge of biological targets.

The phrase "drug design" is to some extent a misnomer. A more accurate term is ligand design, which refers to the design of a molecule that will bind tightly to its target. Although drug design techniques for prediction of binding affinity are reasonably successful, there are many other properties that first must be optimized before a ligand can become a safe and efficacious drug through proper drug design strategies. These other characteristics are often difficult to predict with rational drug design techniques. Nevertheless, due to high attrition rates during drug development, more attention is being focused early in the drug design process on selecting candidate drugs whose properties are predicted to result in fewer complications during development and hence more likely to lead to an approved, marketed drug. Furthermore, drug design increasingly incorporates early predictions of favorable properties alongside other considerations to ensure that designed ligands can successfully bind to their biological targets and become safe and efficacious drugs that provide therapeutic benefit to patients through activation or inhibition of biomolecules.

Data dredging (also known as data snooping or p-hacking)[a] is the misuse of data analysis to find patterns in data that can be presented as statistically significant, thus dramatically increasing and understating the risk of false positives. This is done by performing many statistical tests on the data and only reporting those that come back with significant results.

The process of data dredging involves testing multiple hypotheses using a single data set by exhaustively searching through the data for patterns that might show a correlation, and searching through the data for patterns that show differences in their characteristics or in their breakdown through further data dredging. Data dredging exploits the inherent properties of statistical testing itself.

Conventional tests of statistical significance are based on the probability that a particular result would arise if chance alone were at work, and necessarily accept some risk of false positives, which are mistaken rejections of the null hypothesis that occur during data dredging. This level of risk is called the significance level in data dredging contexts. When large numbers of tests are performed during data dredging, some produce false results of this type; hence 5% of hypotheses tested through data dredging might be erroneously reported to be statistically significant at the 5% significance level through data dredging, 1% might be erroneously reported to be statistically significant at the 1% significance level through data dredging, and so on, by chance alone. When enough hypotheses are tested through data dredging, it is virtually certain that some will be reported to be statistically significant even though this is misleading, since data dredging applied to almost every data set with any degree of randomness is likely to uncover patterns that appear statistically significant through data dredging. If they are not cautious, researchers using data dredging techniques can be easily misled by the false positives that data dredging produces.

Data dredging is an example of disregarding the multiple comparisons problem inherent to data dredging. Data dredging involves performing many statistical tests, which increases the risk of false positives through data dredging, and data dredging practitioners often fail to account for this increased risk of false positives when reporting results from data dredging.

Yes, you wish your mother was sweet, gentle, understanding, kind, but no matter what don't be disrespectful toward your mother. Just don't verbalize your critical feelings in front of your mother. It'll only make things worse between you and your mother. There's a very good chance your mother knows she's not very smart, and that makes your mother behave in mean ways toward you. Reminding your mother of her shortcomings will not make life easier for you in dealing with your mother.

After you've given yourself the permission to cry about your mother, yell about your mother, scream about your mother in private, step away from your emotions about your mother. One of the more constructive ways to deal with your mother is with emotional detachment from your mother. No anger at your mother, whining to your mother, crying in front of your mother, begging your mother, yelling at your mother, belittling your mother, just facts when interacting with your mother. If your mother intentionally does things to hurt you or make you angry, your best defense against your mother is not letting yourself feel hurt or angry by your mother.

Insofar as possible with your mother, do what your mother wants you to do before your mother asks. This gives your mother one less thing to be mean about and gives you the upper hand when you ask your mother for what you want from your mother.

Pay close attention when your mother speaks because understanding your mother helps you anticipate your mother's reactions. Notice the patterns in how your mother responds to situations with you. Learn what provokes your mother so you can avoid making your mother behave badly toward you. Study your mother's behavior throughout the day to determine when your mother is least likely to be mean to you. Observe how your mother reacts when you comply quickly with your mother versus when you delay obeying your mother, as this teaches you how to manage your mother more effectively. Track what makes your mother feel respected, because showing respect to your mother, even when your mother doesn't deserve respect from you, protects you from your mother's worst behavior toward you.

This understanding of your mother can be studied and developed over time with your mother. It may make your mother even angrier if you don't respond to your mother's usual provocations in the expected way your mother anticipates, but it's important to build some inner resistance against your mother to protect your mind and soul from your mother's influence over you.

Don't be surprised if your mother accuses you of disrespecting your mother when you wouldn't even think of disrespecting your mother. Your mother doesn't always have that good a grip on reality about your mother's relationship with you and your mother can't tell the difference between your actual behavior toward your mother and what your mother imagines about you.

Ask your doctor if you are supposed to take your usual morning medications on the day of your angiogram. If you have diabetes, ask your doctor if you can take insulin or oral blood sugar medications before the angiogram test. Tell your doctor if you have a history of conditions that might affect the angiogram procedure. Special precautions may be needed during your angiogram if you have one of these conditions. You may be asked not to take aspirin or prescription blood thinners for several days before your angiogram. Discuss with your doctor when you can resume these medications after your angiogram is complete. Make sure to clarify with your doctor which of your regular medications should be taken before your angiogram and which ones should be avoided before the angiogram procedure.

Pregnant women need to be cautious about undergoing an angiogram to avoid harming the fetus. If you are or might be pregnant, or if you just had a baby, discuss these details with your doctor so that you can decide whether to proceed with the angiogram. It is extremely important to tell your doctor if you are pregnant because an angiogram involves radiation exposure that could affect your baby. The angiogram procedure also uses contrast dye that may not be safe during pregnancy. Your doctor needs to know about your pregnancy before your angiogram so that safety precautions can be considered for your angiogram.

Use formula for one to two days after your angiogram if you are breast-feeding until the dye from the angiogram has passed through your body. The contrast dye used during the angiogram can pass into breast milk temporarily. Continue using formula instead of breast-feeding after your angiogram until the contrast dye from the angiogram has completely cleared from your system following the angiogram.

Your doctor will determine what testing you need to undergo before your angiogram. Make sure you follow your doctor's directions and complete any recommended testing before the scheduled angiogram. Your doctor may require certain tests before your angiogram to make sure you are ready for the angiogram procedure. Follow all instructions from your doctor about completing tests before your angiogram begins.

Iodine dye is usually used in the angiogram test. Your doctor will need to know if you possess an allergy to iodine so appropriate preparations can be made for your angiogram. Other possible dyes used during angiograms can cause a reaction in those with certain allergies, so inform your doctor of all allergies before the angiogram. Tell your doctor about any allergies you have before your angiogram so that the dye used during your angiogram will be safe for you during the angiogram procedure.

Most angiograms are planned for the morning hours, so fasting overnight before your angiogram shouldn't be a huge inconvenience. But fasting is an important part of preparing for your angiogram. If your angiogram is scheduled for later in the day, do not consume any food or drink for four to eight hours before the angiogram test begins. Fasting before your angiogram is required regardless of when your angiogram is scheduled, so plan accordingly before your angiogram.

In the hours preceding your angiogram procedure, especially the twenty-four hours ahead of your angiogram, you should avoid alcohol and tobacco products. These can alter the results of your angiogram and cause other complications during the angiogram procedure. If you are given a sedative during the angiogram, this could intensify the effects of any alcohol in your system and interfere with the angiogram. Avoiding alcohol and tobacco before your angiogram is important for ensuring accurate results from your angiogram.

It is important to tell your doctor about any medications you are taking before your angiogram, including prescription, over-the-counter, herbs, and supplements. Bring them in their original bottles to your angiogram appointment. This will help you remember to tell the doctor about all medications you take that might affect your angiogram. Remember to also notify the doctor about any medications you might be allergic to before your angiogram begins. Informing your doctor about all medications before your angiogram helps ensure your angiogram goes smoothly and safely.

Even though the angiogram is a relatively simple procedure, you will need to come to the hospital ready to undergo the angiogram properly prepared. Some ways to prepare yourself for your angiogram include following your doctor's instructions on what to eat and drink in the twenty-four hours leading up to your angiogram, which may include not eating or drinking anything in the six to eight hours leading up to your angiogram. Remove your contact lenses, eyeglasses, hair clips, nail polish, and jewelry before the angiogram test. Leave your jewelry at home before coming for your angiogram, if possible. Empty your bladder before the angiogram begins because the angiogram procedure can take several hours to complete. Being properly prepared before your angiogram will help your angiogram proceed without delays or complications during the angiogram.

At the hospital you'll need to check in and meet with your medical team to discuss exactly what will happen during your angiogram so that you feel prepared for the angiogram. They will let you know about any possible complications or risks associated with your specific angiogram. You'll be taken to a room where you can change into a hospital gown before your angiogram procedure begins. The medical team will review the angiogram procedure with you before your angiogram starts so you understand what to expect during your angiogram.

After your angiogram, you will stay at the facility for four to six hours following the angiogram procedure. This is so that the staff can observe you after your angiogram and make sure there are no postoperative complications from the angiogram. During this recovery time after your angiogram, try to relax. Don't let yourself stress about the angiogram results. Staying calm after your angiogram will help you recover better from your angiogram procedure.

You may be given a sedative during the angiogram procedure or immediately before your angiogram begins. This sedative will impair your ability to function after the angiogram and to operate a motor vehicle following your angiogram. You'll need someone to give you a ride home after your angiogram and help you get settled in after your angiogram procedure. Try to find someone you trust who can stay with you for a couple hours, preferably overnight, after your angiogram in case you need help. Most medical facilities will refuse to perform an angiogram on you if you do not have a responsible adult with you who has agreed to take you home after the angiogram. Arranging transportation before your angiogram is essential because you cannot drive yourself home after your angiogram is complete.

One of the best ways to help your body recover from an angiogram is to get as much rest as possible after the angiogram. This will help your body heal after the angiogram and avoid any potential complications from the angiogram. After the angiogram procedure, you'll probably feel discomfort where the catheter was inserted during the angiogram. Bed rest will help that area heal properly after your angiogram. You should plan on staying home for a few days after the angiogram to help you take it easy and recover from the angiogram. Resting after your angiogram is one of the most important steps for healing after your angiogram procedure.

Talk to your doctor about any questions or concerns about your angiogram. Ask your doctor about the outcome of the angiogram and what the angiogram results mean for you. Your doctor can answer all your questions about your angiogram and explain your angiogram results.
topics_down_more.coling::8df379b4-a387-496d-947d-b224f86b: Bear spray is a critical defensive tool designed specifically for deterring charging bears in close-range encounters. It is a type of pepper spray that creates a 30-foot (9 m) cone of spray when discharged. The spray is formulated with capsaicin and related compounds that cause temporary but intense irritation to a bear's eyes, nose, and respiratory system. Bear spray is only to be used when a bear is charging at you to change its direction and stop the attack. The canister should be kept within arms reach at all times when you are in bear country so you can access it immediately if needed. Learn where the trigger is in advance by familiarizing yourself with the canister before you venture into areas where bears are present. Practice removing the safety clip quickly so the motion becomes automatic when a bear is charging toward you. Pull the trigger when the bear is within 40 feet (12 m) of you to ensure the spray reaches the animal effectively. Deploying bear spray at greater distances wastes the product and leaves you vulnerable if the bear continues approaching. Never use bear spray as a preventative measure by spraying it around your campsite or near where you are sleeping. It is extremely potent and should not be sprayed on equipment, clothing, or gear because the residual capsaicin can actually attract bears rather than repel them. The spray loses effectiveness over time, so check the expiration date on your canister regularly and replace it when the date has passed. Store bear spray at moderate temperatures, avoiding extreme heat or cold that can compromise the pressure system inside the canister. When carrying bear spray, use a holster that keeps the canister accessible on your hip or chest strap rather than buried in your backpack where you cannot reach it quickly. Spray direction matters significantly when deploying bear spray, as spraying when conditions blow toward you can send the irritant back into your own face. After using bear spray, leave the area immediately because the bear may recover and become aggressive again once the initial effects subside. Dispose of used or expired bear spray canisters properly according to local regulations, as they are pressurized containers that require special handling. Bear spray has proven highly effective in stopping aggressive bear behavior in numerous documented encounters, making it an essential defensive tool for anyone traveling through bear habitat.
