Pick a time when they are in a good mood. Avoid approaching them right after a hard day at work. Try to figure out their mood by asking, "How was your day?" Choose a time when you will not be interrupted or competing for their attention with other people or issues. Right after dinner or before bed is usually a pretty peaceful and private time. You want to select a moment when they seem relaxed and open to conversation, not distracted or preoccupied with other concerns. Pay attention to their body language and overall demeanor before initiating this important discussion. If they seem tense or worried, it might be better to wait for another opportunity when they appear more receptive. Look for signs that indicate they are in a calm state of mind and ready to have a meaningful conversation with you.

If you don't get a chance at home, you can also talk with them in a different setting where they might be more relaxed and receptive to conversation. You might say, "Dad, do you want to spend some time together? I have some things I'd like to talk with you about." Sometimes a change of location can make difficult conversations feel more comfortable and less confrontational. A different setting can reduce tension and make both parties feel more at ease during the discussion. You can always talk with just one parent too and ask them to approach the other one, if needed. This works best if you know your mom, for example, is a bit more lenient or if you feel closer to her. Consider which parent might be more understanding or easier to talk to initially, and use that relationship as a starting point for your conversation.

Staying honest and straightforward during your conversation with them is just one way to show your maturity. So, don't tell lies, even white lies, when you talk with them about this matter. If they ask you direct questions, answer them truthfully and completely. If you are caught in a lie you will lose any ground that you've gained with them. Your credibility is essential to maintaining their trust throughout this discussion and beyond. Being truthful demonstrates that you take this conversation seriously and respect them enough to be honest.

Another part of honesty in your conversation with them is your being open to their concerns so you can respond to them thoughtfully. Listen carefully when they express worries or reservations about what you're asking. Acknowledge their perspective and show that you understand why they might have these concerns. This demonstrates emotional maturity and respect for their point of view. Being receptive to what they say shows that you value their input in this important discussion.

Avoid comparing yourself with others during your talk with them if it involves exaggeration. For example, don't tell your parents that your best friend has been in a similar situation for the past two years, unless it is really true. Your parents will sense that you are not being honest and can easily check the facts. Stick to discussing your own situation and your own readiness rather than trying to justify your position by pointing to what others are doing. Focus on your own circumstances and why you believe you are ready for what you're requesting.

To get what you want from them, you may have to give a little. If your parents agree to your request, they will most likely place some conditions on their agreement. If these are promises that you can actually keep, it is best to say yes. You can also bring up compromises as a way to bring your parents back to the bargaining table if they say no initially. This will create an opening for greater freedom in the future as you gain their trust. Think about what concessions you're willing to make before you even start the conversation, so you're prepared to negotiate thoughtfully. Being flexible about conditions shows your willingness to meet them halfway.

Many of the conditions they set will involve demonstrating your responsibility and maturity to them. Be prepared to accept reasonable limitations they propose. These are all expectations that show you understand the gravity of what you're asking and that you're willing to meet them halfway. Consider their perspective and what would make them feel more comfortable granting your request. Understanding why they might want certain conditions helps you respond to their concerns appropriately.

Try to control your emotions during your talk with them. Avoid yelling, crying, whining, or begging. A temper tantrum of any kind will make them lose all respect for your position. To stay calm, repeat in your head the word "control" or "calm." Count for five seconds, in your head, before you answer any questions or make any statements you may regret. Take deep breaths if you feel yourself becoming emotional or upset during the discussion. Maintaining your composure throughout the conversation demonstrates the maturity you're trying to prove to them.

Make sure to watch your tone with them as well. It is really easy to say nice words with a sarcastic attitude. For example, "That's great," sounds really different depending on your tone of voice. Be mindful of how you're coming across to them throughout the entire conversation. Your tone can undermine even the most carefully chosen words if you're not careful about how you deliver them. If you feel increasingly frustrated by the conversation with them, plan a way to manage those feelings constructively afterward rather than letting frustration show during the discussion itself.

Your parents will most likely have quite a bit to say back to you, so make sure to pay close attention to what they are saying. Look into their eyes when they are talking. This will help to show that you are not embarrassed or ashamed to talk about your request. Nod your head when they make good points and even smile if you really agree with something. Show them through your body language that you respect their input and value their wisdom. Your nonverbal communication is just as important as the words you say during this conversation with them.

A big part of active listening to them is asking questions. If they say no to you, respond by asking, "Why not?" Tell them that you honestly want to understand their perspective in this situation. This will help you to figure out what is bothering them so you can work on addressing their concerns. Press them gently for specifics so you know exactly what you need to do to earn their approval. Understanding their reasoning gives you a path forward even if they initially refuse your request.

If you just can't talk to your parents face-to-face, you may need to write down your feelings and thoughts via a letter to them. This is also a good idea if you think your parents may have an extreme reaction to your request. Make sure that your letter to them is well written and calm. Do not write anything that you will regret. Instead of writing something confrontational, frame your letter in respectful, measured terms that demonstrate the same maturity you would show in a face-to-face conversation. It may be helpful to show your letter to someone you trust for feedback before presenting it to your parents so you can ensure it conveys the right tone.

Trapdoor spiders are approximately 0.79 to 1.26 inches (1 to 3 cm) long, which means roughly between the size of your pinky nail and your thumbnail. Trapdoor spiders are black or brown, with stout bodies and legs. Some trapdoor spider species have paler color markings, or they may have a silky covering of hair on their bodies. Trapdoor spider bodies are divided into two sections: the thorax (containing the head and legs) and the abdomen. The abdomen of a trapdoor spider is typically lighter and a slightly different color from the thorax.

The small size of trapdoor spiders can make them difficult to observe, but a trapdoor spider will have 6 eyes arranged in 3 groups. Trapdoor spiders have bodies that are less hairy and smaller compared to their relatives. Trapdoor spiders also have shinier bodies. The jaws of a trapdoor spider are attached to the front of its head. Trapdoor spider jaws move up and down.

Female trapdoor spiders are larger than the male trapdoor spiders, but you will seldom see female trapdoor spiders because they rarely leave their burrows. Therefore, if you see a trapdoor spider, it is most likely a male trapdoor spider. Look for these characteristics that identify male trapdoor spiders: short and blunt spinnerets, which produce silk and are located at the tip of the abdomen of trapdoor spiders; a double spur about halfway along their front legs; a dusty or dull carapace (a harder area covering much of the thorax of trapdoor spiders) that is lightly covered in bristles; and pedipalps (small appendages near the jaws of trapdoor spiders) that resemble boxing gloves.

There are numerous varieties of trapdoor spiders, each trapdoor spider variety with slightly different physical characteristics. More varieties of trapdoor spiders are still being discovered by researchers studying trapdoor spiders. If you think you have seen a trapdoor spider, look up the specific varieties of trapdoor spiders that live in your area, so that you know what kind of specific markings to expect on trapdoor spiders. Different trapdoor spider varieties may have variations in the color markings on their bodies. The physical characteristics of trapdoor spiders can vary between the different varieties of trapdoor spiders.

Trapdoor spiders favor warm environments. Trapdoor spiders will burrow in grassy areas, hillsides, and dirt embankments. Trapdoor spiders burrow in the ground, creating holes about 0.75 inches wide and up to 8 inches deep. Trapdoor spiders cover their burrow with a silken hinged "trapdoor" camouflaged by sticks, pebbles, and other natural material. Because the burrows of trapdoor spiders are camouflaged, trapdoor spider burrows can be very hard to see. Larger trapdoor spider burrows may have multiple trapdoors. Usually, the burrow of a trapdoor spider faces sunlight and will be found near vegetation. The burrows of trapdoor spiders are carefully constructed underground homes.

Trapdoor spiders are shy and are rarely seen far from their burrows. Male trapdoor spiders may wander during mating season, however. You might be able to spy a trapdoor spider when it eats. Trapdoor spiders will wait in their burrows until they sense vibrations in the ground. Then, trapdoor spiders will leap out of the trapdoor, grab prey, and drag it back into the burrow. Trapdoor spiders spend most of their lives within their burrows. Trapdoor spiders are solitary creatures that remain in their underground homes. Trapdoor spiders stay hidden in their carefully constructed burrows for the majority of their lives.

Corfe Castle railway station is a railway station located in the village of Corfe Castle, in the English county of Dorset. Originally an intermediate station on the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch line from Wareham to Swanage, the line and station were closed by British Rail in 1972. It has since reopened as a station on the Swanage Railway, a heritage railway that runs from Norden station just north of Corfe Castle to Swanage station. The station serves as an important stopping point on this heritage line and provides access to the historic village of Corfe Castle.

Corfe Castle station is on a railway line connecting Wareham and Norden, providing essential rail service through this section of the Isle of Purbeck.

History
The position of Corfe Castle station, commanding the only relatively low level route across the hilly spine of the Isle of Purbeck, meant that the railway line passed close to the centre of the village. Corfe Castle station was built for the opening of the Swanage Railway line on 20 May 1885, following the receipt of its Act in 1881. From its opening, the railway line and Corfe Castle station were operated by the L&SWR, and the line was absorbed into that railway company in 1886. 

Corfe Castle station was the only intermediate station on the Swanage branch line, a status it retained throughout its operational history until closure by British Rail. The station possessed the only passing loop between the junction with the main line at Worgret Junction and Swanage station, making it a crucial operational point on the branch line. The operational importance of Corfe Castle station on the Swanage branch line meant it served as the single most critical intermediate point for train operations between Worgret Junction and Swanage station throughout the period when the station remained open under railway company operation. The significance of Corfe Castle station's position on the branch line was reinforced by its status as the sole intermediate stopping point with passing facilities on this section of railway.

Closure of Corfe Castle station was first proposed in 1967, and despite local opposition the station and line finally closed on 3 January 1972. During the final few years of Corfe Castle station's operation under British Rail, passenger train services calling at the station were operated by diesel electric multiple units serving the branch line through Corfe Castle.

From the time of the first proposal of closure, a campaign to reopen Corfe Castle station and the railway as a heritage railway developed. Most of the track bed, including Corfe Castle station site, was bought by Dorset County Council. Proposals to use the railway route through Corfe Castle as a road bypass for the village were eventually rejected by the county council in 1986, preserving the station site for potential railway use. In the meantime the Swanage Railway had started operating a steam service at the Swanage end of the line in 1982, gradually working toward reopening Corfe Castle station. The preservation efforts for Corfe Castle station continued steadily as the heritage railway extended its operations northward from Swanage, bringing the reopening of Corfe Castle station closer to reality with each passing year of restoration work on the line.

There were concerns that reopening Corfe Castle station as a northern terminus for the Swanage Railway would cause parking problems in the village surrounding the station. It was therefore decided to extend the line a further half a mile north from Corfe Castle station to a new station site. Here the new Norden station was built and most trains terminate there rather than at Corfe Castle station. Corfe Castle station itself reopened on 12 August 1995, although the official opening of the restored station was not until February of the following year. The reopening of Corfe Castle station marked a significant milestone in the restoration of the railway line, with the station once again serving passengers traveling through Corfe Castle on the heritage railway.

A project by Swanage Railway volunteers to install a footbridge across the running lines between the platforms at Corfe Castle station was completed in April 2007, when the official opening of this new station facility took place. The footbridge installed at Corfe Castle station was originally built in 1893 by a railway company. With cast-iron columns and a wrought iron span, the footbridge spent its previous life at another station before being removed by Swanage Railway volunteers and relocated to Corfe Castle station. The footbridge can accommodate the people who now use Corfe Castle station, and is safer and more convenient for passengers at the station than crossing over the track via the gated and locked foot crossing that previously served Corfe Castle station. The footbridge project at Corfe Castle station won heritage awards in December 2007, with recognition presented to the civil engineer of the Swanage Railway and his team of volunteers who worked on the Corfe Castle station footbridge. The completion of the footbridge at Corfe Castle station represented another important improvement to the facilities available to passengers using the heritage railway at Corfe Castle.

Railway services operated to and from Corfe Castle station in summer 2018 and 2019, connecting it to Wareham, with services continuing to other destinations. There were also services on Saturdays and Sundays between Wareham and Swanage calling at Corfe Castle station in summer 2018 and 2019, operated with trains stopping at the station. However, in July 2019 these services calling at Corfe Castle station were stopped and there are currently no such services to Corfe Castle station.

Services at Corfe Castle station
Services at Corfe Castle station run every day from the beginning of April to late October, with weekend only operation at the station in March, November and December. The level of service at Corfe Castle station varies from 6 to 17 trains a day in each direction, depending on the season and the day of the week. Southbound from Corfe Castle station, trains operate to stations at Harman's Cross, Herston, and Swanage. Northbound from Corfe Castle station, trains operate to Norden station, reached in just 3 minutes from Corfe Castle. The service pattern at Corfe Castle station provides regular connections throughout the operating season, ensuring that passengers can travel conveniently from Corfe Castle station to other stations on the heritage railway line.

Museum at Corfe Castle station
Corfe Castle station is also the home of the Swanage Railway's Railway Museum, which is housed in the old goods shed at Corfe Castle station and an adjacent rail van located at the station. The museum at Corfe Castle station is open on most operating days when trains are running through the station. The museum at Corfe Castle station includes a steam locomotive, which is displayed at the station and forms part of the collection housed at Corfe Castle station. The museum at Corfe Castle station provides visitors to the heritage railway with an opportunity to learn more about railway history while visiting Corfe Castle station.

Matt Wozniak (born January 6, 1983) is a Canadian curler from Winnipeg, Manitoba. He currently plays second on Team Jason Gunnlaugson. Wozniak is the former second for the Mike McEwen team which curled out of the Assiniboine Memorial Curling Club in Winnipeg.

Career

2005–2010
In 2005, Wozniak joined the new Mike McEwen rink that included Justin Richter and Andrew Melnuk as fellow members of the curling team. For the 2006-07 curling season, Richter and Melnuk left the curling team and were replaced with curlers Geordie Hargreaves and Adam Guenther. The curling team disbanded after just one season of competitive curling together.

Wozniak and McEwen joined with brothers Denni and B. J. Neufeld in 2007 to form a new competitive curling team. In their first curling season together, they were a semi-finalist at the 2008 Safeway Championship, Manitoba's provincial curling championship. They competed at their first Grand Slam curling event as a team at the end of the curling season, at the 2008 Players' Championships curling event. The curling team won two games at the curling event, before being eliminated from the curling competition.

At the conclusion of the 2008-09 curling season the McEwen curling team was ranked 7th on the Canadian Curling Association rankings. The curling team had made it to three Grand Slam curling playoffs, and finished 4th at the 2009 Safeway Championship curling event.

During the 'Road to the Roar' 2009 curling qualifier event, the McEwen curling team just lost out to fellow Manitoba curlers on the Jason Gunnlaugson curling team in the semi-finals of the curling competition. The McEwen curling team thus missed out on the curling trials final despite being the favourite in that particular curling matchup versus the Gunnlaugson curling team.

McEwen's curling rink made it to his first provincial curling final in 2010, when the curling team lost to Jeff Stoughton's curling team in the 2010 Manitoba provincial curling final. The curling game was being played in Steinbach, Manitoba and as the Neufeld brothers and their father have roots in Steinbach, the McEwen curling team were treated very much as the home team and crowd favourites at the curling event.

2010-2015: Grand Slam curling success and perennial provincial curling runner-up
The McEwen curling team started the 2010-11 curling season off well by defeating provincial curling rival Jeff Stoughton's curling team to win the curling championship and his first ever Grand Slam curling title in November, 2010. In part because of the curling team's runner-up result in the provincial curling finals of 2010 and in part because of his 4 curling victories and leading the overall money winnings in the curling season as of November 2010, the McEwen curling team was named as a nominee for the provincial curling team of the year by the Manitoba curling association.

The curling team continued their strong curling season that year by defeating provincial curling rival Stoughton's curling team in the semi-final of the 2011 Canadian curling event. The curling team would then go on to beat the Glenn Howard curling team in the extra end of the final, thus winning their second career Grand Slam curling event and their second curling championship of that season.

Wozniak's curling rink once again made it to the Manitoba provincial curling championship this time, being the top seed curling team (also ranked 1st in Canada for curling). However, the curling team once again lost to Stoughton's curling team in the final of the 2011 Safeway Championship curling event, losing by one point in the final end. The McEwen curling team then lost their third straight provincial curling final game at the 2012 Safeway Championship, this time losing to Rob Fowler's curling team, thus tying a provincial curling record for consecutive curling final losses previously set by curler Kerry Burtnyk. This dubious curling record was avoided in 2013, when the McEwen curling rink failed to reach the curling final, but again losing to the rival Stoughton curling rink in the 2013 Safeway Championship curling semi-final. Once again, at the 2014 Safeway Championship curling event, the curling team lost the final to Stoughton's curling team.

Despite being ranked first in the curling rankings and on the money list for curling, Wozniak lost his fifth provincial curling final in six years in 2015, losing to Reid Carruthers' curling team.

Provincial curling title and curling team breakup 
Wozniak's curling rink won their first provincial curling title in 2016, sending the curling team to their first Brier curling championship. The Matt Dunstone curling rink had committed themselves to the curling championships, which occurred at the same time as the 2016 Tim Hortons Brier, so when the Dunstone curling rink beat Reid Carruthers' curling team in the semi-final, McEwen's curling team would go to the Brier, even if the curling team had lost to Dunstone's curling rink.

In 2017, Wozniak defended his Manitoba curling Championship by beating Reid Carruthers' curling team in the final. Wozniak would then better his 2016 Brier curling showing, going 9–2 in the curling round robin to enter the curling playoffs in first place and with hammer and choice of curling rocks (Brad Gushue's curling team was also 9–2 but lost first place due to losing his curling round robin meeting with the Manitoba curling team). Wozniak's curling team then lost 7–5 to Brad Gushue's curling team in the 1 vs. 2 curling game. In the curling semi finals against Kevin Koe's curling team, Wozniak's curling team was in control for most of the curling game, being up 5–3 with hammer in the eighth end, but Koe's curling team made a comeback with a steal in the eighth end, two points in the tenth end, and another steal in the extra end, dropping the Manitoba curling team to the bronze medal curling game. The curling team recovered to win their first Brier curling medal, defeating Brad Jacobs' curling team in their curling rematch, 7–6 in an extra end.

While competing at the 2018 Viterra Championship curling event, skip McEwen came down with illness and was unable to play curling after the first curling game. B. J. Neufeld skipped the curling team, until a surprise appearance by McEwen in the curling final, where the curling team lost to Carruthers' curling team. Despite the curling setback, the curling team still had a chance to qualify for the 2018 Tim Hortons Brier through the wildcard curling game, which the curling team won over Jason Gunnlaugson's curling team. The McEwen curling team had a difficult Brier and alongside Carruthers' curling team was unable to qualify for the curling playoffs. Following the Brier curling championship, the McEwen curling team announced the curling team would be breaking up at the end of the 2017–18 curling season. Just days after the curling announcement, the McEwen curling team won the 2018 curling championship, winning the top prize money, and was the first curling team to go through the entire curling event undefeated. The curling victory was the curling team's seventh overall.

Wozniak took a few years off from curling play after the McEwen curling team broke up. However, Wozniak played curling with Marlene Albrecht and spared for McEwen's new curling team. After Alex Forrest stepped away from competitive curling after the 2019–20 curling season, Wozniak joined the Jason Gunnlaugson curling rink. Due to the pandemic in Manitoba, the 2021 provincial curling championship was cancelled. As the Gunnlaugson curling team were the reigning provincial curling champions, the curling team was chosen to represent Manitoba at the curling championship. The Gunnlaugson curling team competed at the curling championship with Wozniak as second on the curling team. The curling team finished with a respectable curling record during the curling round robin. Wozniak continued playing second for the Gunnlaugson curling team in subsequent curling seasons. The Gunnlaugson curling team competed in multiple provincial curling championships with Wozniak on the curling roster. Wozniak's role as second on the Gunnlaugson curling team proved valuable to the curling team's overall curling performance. The curling team participated in various curling events throughout Manitoba with Wozniak playing second. Wozniak's curling experience from his years with the McEwen curling team benefited the Gunnlaugson curling team. The curling team continued to compete at the provincial curling level with Wozniak as a key member of the curling roster.

Operation Claw was a joint Swedish–American intelligence operation, with Norwegian support, that was carried out at Lillehammer shortly after the German capitulation by the end of World War II. The operation involved transferring thirty-five German intelligence specialists along with various equipment first to Sweden and then to U.S. camps in occupied Germany through an agreement between the Americans and the German High Command of the Wehrmacht in Norway. The intelligence material secured through Operation Claw became very useful for the Americans during the early Cold War period, providing valuable information that would assist American intelligence efforts in the postwar era. Operation Claw was controversial both when it happened and afterwards, raising questions about sovereignty, alliance obligations, and the boundaries of acceptable intelligence gathering in the immediate postwar period. The operation was particularly sensitive because the Americans were operating in what was seen as a British controlled country, and because they were securing information in cooperation with neutral Sweden, making the entire undertaking diplomatically problematic for all parties involved.

The planning and execution of Operation Claw began even before the war in Europe ended, as American intelligence organisations sought German intelligence experts with knowledge that would prove valuable to American postwar intelligence efforts. American officials immediately after the war in Europe ended began to cooperate with German intelligence personnel who possessed the expertise that American intelligence services desired. Operation Claw was part of an organized effort to obtain as much German intelligence information and personnel as possible, an effort focused on securing these valuable assets before other allied powers could claim them. The operation was conducted with great secrecy because the war was still being fought, the US and the Soviet Union were still officially allies, and the allies had designated Norway as part of the British sphere of influence. Both for the US and the neutral Sweden, Operation Claw was thus diplomatically very sensitive and required careful concealment from both the British and the Soviets, making secrecy absolutely essential to the operation's success.

At the Wehrmacht camp at Lillehammer, a group of 35 German experts on signals intelligence had been gathered who possessed extensive knowledge that American intelligence services sought to acquire. In cooperation with the American intelligence organisation Office of Strategic Services (OSS) and with knowledge and support from the Norwegian legation in Stockholm, agents for the Swedish intelligence organisation C-byrån traveled together with two Norwegian intelligence specialists to Lillehammer on May 9 and 10, 1945. The German group of experts were taken out of the camp and transported to Sweden as part of Operation Claw. After a few weeks in Sweden they were on June 12 flown from Torslanda Airport close to Gothenburg to US occupied Germany and were interned in an American military camp at Wiesbaden. The transfer of the German experts at Lillehammer through Operation Claw was directed from the highest level, with Major General William J. Donovan leading from the U.S. side and Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd serving as chief of the Defense Staff from the Swedish side, ensuring that Operation Claw had the necessary high-level authorization and oversight.

More than a month after the German capitulation, a British led search supported by Norwegian personnel was executed to find German key personnel hiding in German military camps at Lillehammer and elsewhere in Norway. The search force soon became aware that a number of German key personnel had been removed in Operation Claw a month earlier. Operation Claw had successfully extracted these valuable intelligence assets before the British-led search could locate them at Lillehammer. This discovery raised questions about the propriety of Operation Claw and whether it had undermined the broader allied effort to account for German intelligence personnel who had been stationed at Lillehammer. The secrecy surrounding Operation Claw meant that even allied personnel conducting subsequent searches were unaware that key German intelligence specialists had already been removed from Lillehammer. This lack of coordination highlighted the tensions that Operation Claw both reflected and exacerbated among the wartime allies conducting operations in Norway.

Operation Claw was the beginning of postwar era cooperation between Swedish and US intelligence services, marking a significant shift in violation of Sweden's officially stated neutrality. From the American side Operation Claw was viewed as a great success and the responsible officers within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, were both honored with decorations where Operation Claw specifically was mentioned in the citations. The success of Operation Claw from the American perspective was measured both by the intelligence materials obtained from Lillehammer and by the successful recruitment of German experts who had been extracted from the Wehrmacht camp. For the Swedish C-byrån, however, Operation Claw quickly became toxic and problematic, threatening Sweden's carefully maintained neutrality. Even though Operation Claw was to be kept confidential, information about the operation leaked to the Swedish press, creating a political scandal that damaged C-byrån's standing. The exposure of Operation Claw and Sweden's violation of neutrality led to C-byrån being dissolved in February 1946. The dissolution of C-byrån demonstrated the high political costs that Operation Claw carried for Sweden, even as it brought intelligence benefits to the Americans who had initiated the operation.

Information regarding Operation Claw continued to be classified as confidential in the post-war years and some of it still remains classified today. A report about Operation Claw in the British National Archives was restricted until 2020, demonstrating the lasting sensitivity of the operation and its diplomatic implications. The continued classification of materials related to Operation Claw decades after its execution at Lillehammer suggests that the operation involved methods or outcomes that governments still consider too sensitive for public disclosure. Operation Claw thus remains partially obscured from historical scrutiny, with its full dimensions and consequences still not entirely known to researchers seeking to understand the operation's complete impact.

Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon directed by Earl Duvall. The short was released on February 17, 1934 and received production number 6125.

The film was supervised by Earl Duvall, who handled the directorial responsibilities for this Merrie Melodies entry. The characters were animated by Jack King and Frank Tipper, both of whom received credit for their animation work on Honeymoon Hotel, as well as Bob Clampett, Paul Fennell, Chuck Jones and Frank Tashlin, whose contributions to the cartoon went uncredited. Jack King and Frank Tipper were the animators who received official credit for animating the characters in Honeymoon Hotel. The music score was composed by Bernard Brown, who received sole credit, and Norman Spencer, who composed music but remained uncredited for his work on Honeymoon Hotel. Bernard Brown was the composer who received official credit for the music score of Honeymoon Hotel. The sound was recorded by Bernard Brown, though he went uncredited for this particular contribution to the cartoon.

The plot of Honeymoon Hotel follows a male and female bug who check into a hotel which subsequently catches on fire during their stay at the establishment. The narrative centers on these two bug characters and their experience at the hotel that catches fire.

The film is notable for being the first Warner Bros. cartoon produced in color, marking a significant milestone in the studio's animation history. Honeymoon Hotel used the Cinecolor process since another studio held exclusive rights to a different color process at that time. Only one other Merrie Melodies cartoon was produced in Cinecolor before the Merrie Melodies series briefly returned to black-and-white production. Eventually, the Merrie Melodies series transitioned to a different color process for its color cartoons. The Cinecolor process made a return appearance in Warner Bros. animation production before being phased out permanently.

Modern Greek art is art from the period between the emergence of the new independent Greek state and the 20th century. As Mainland Greece was under Ottoman rule for all four centuries, Greek artistic development was hindered and Greek creative expression was suppressed, preventing Greek artists from participating in the Renaissance and artistic movements that transformed other European nations. Greek islands such as Crete and the Ionian islands experienced different conditions that allowed Greek artistic traditions to persist and evolve, as these Greek territories were under Venetian or other European powers' rule, enabling Greek painters and sculptors in those regions to assimilate radical artistic changes while maintaining Greek cultural identity. The Cretan School represents an important Greek artistic movement that developed distinctive Greek visual language, and the Heptanese School of art represents another important Greek artistic movement that cultivated Greek aesthetic sensibilities through techniques absorbed from broader European culture.

Modern Greek art developed its distinctive character through the particular socioeconomic conditions of Greece itself, shaped fundamentally by Greek historical circumstances and Greek cultural aspirations. The large Greek diaspora across Europe influenced Greek artistic development, as Greek artists abroad maintained connections to Greek themes and Greek subject matter. The new Greek social elite patronized Greek artists and supported Greek artistic institutions, fostering Greek cultural revival through visual arts. Greek painting and Greek sculpture absorbed influences from Greek historical circumstances, yet Greek artists transformed these circumstances into distinctively Greek expressions that reflected Greek cultural aspirations and Greek aesthetic sensibilities.

Modern Greek art began to develop when Greek artists absorbed many elements while creating a distinctive style of Greek art reflecting Greek cultural identity. Greek historical circumstances inspired Greek painters, as did Greece's geography and Greece's history, providing Greek artists with profound subject matter rooted in Greek experience and Greek cultural aspirations. After centuries of Ottoman rule, few opportunities for education in the arts existed in newly independent Greece, so Greek artists studied abroad while maintaining Greek cultural consciousness and Greek thematic concerns. Munich became an important international center where the majority of Greek artists of the 19th century chose to study, and Greek students learned true fresco techniques for Greek mural paintings on fresh wet lime plaster, techniques that Greek artists would later apply to Greek artistic institutions. During this period much Greek art was emotional and theatrical in tone, reflecting Greek aspirations and Greek struggles and Greek historical circumstances. The most prominent themes of Greek artists studying in Munich included Greek urban life, Greek rural life, Greek still life subjects, and Greek landscape painting, all reflecting Greek cultural identity and Greek aesthetic sensibilities.

Greek artists would return to Greece and pass on their knowledge to younger Greek students, establishing Greek artistic institutions and Greek educational frameworks that would foster Greek cultural revival. Some Greek artists remained in Munich, developing the Greek "Munich School" of painting through academic and personal bonds between Greek painters and Greek cultural consciousness. Nikolaos Gysis became an important Greek teacher and Greek artist, soon becoming a leading figure among Greek artists and Greek cultural ambassadors who maintained Greek thematic concerns. Greek academism, Greek realism, Greek genre painting, Greek upper middle class portraiture, Greek still life and Greek landscape painting often represented features within Greek aesthetic frameworks that reflected Greek cultural identity. These Greek artistic modes would be replaced by Greek aesthetic sensibilities that Greek artists like Nikolaos Gysis explored, maintaining Greek cultural consciousness while developing Greek artistic expression. Greek artistic development continued through significant Greek artists who explored Greek themes through Greek visual language rooted in Greek experience.

Many Greek artists of the Munich School chose subjects depicting Greek everyday life, Greek local customs, and Greek living conditions, documenting Greek society through visual representation that reflected Greek cultural aspirations. Several important Greek painters emerged during this formative period of Greek art, each contributing to Greek aesthetic sensibilities. Theodoros Vryzakis, a prominent Greek painter, specialized in Greek historical painting especially inspired by the 1821 Greek War of Independence, creating powerful images of Greek heroism and Greek sacrifice that embodied Greek cultural identity. Nikiphoros Lytras, another significant Greek artist, concentrated on realistic depictions of Greek life, portraying Greek people in Greek settings with Greek authenticity that reflected Greek thematic concerns. Georgios Jakobides, an accomplished Greek painter, devoted his attention to Greek infants and Greek children, later becoming the first Director of the new National Gallery of Athens, a crucial Greek cultural institution that would foster Greek artistic development. Georgios Roilos was another leading Greek painter of the period closely associated with Greek aesthetic sensibilities and Greek cultural consciousness. Konstantinos Volanakis, a celebrated Greek maritime painter, was inspired by the Greek sea, capturing Greek coastal scenes and Greek nautical traditions that reflected Greek experience.

Other Greek artists associated with Greek artistic institutions included Symeon Sabbides, whose Greek subjects reflected Greek sensibilities and Greek cultural identity, and Yannoulis Chalepas, a Greek sculptor of exceptional talent who maintained Greek thematic concerns. Leonidas Drosis contributed to Greek sculpture and Greek architectural ornament that reflected Greek aesthetic sensibilities, along with several Greek artists who maintained Greek cultural consciousness, including Theofrastos Triantafyllidis, who brought Greek perspectives to Greek artistic expression, and Jorgos Busianis, who explored Greek themes through Greek visual language rooted in Greek experience. Even Giorgio de Chirico, though developing reputation beyond Greece, maintained Greek cultural connections to Greek aesthetic frameworks.

Notable Greek sculptors of the new Greek Kingdom included Leonidas Drosis, whose major work was extensive neo-classical Greek architectural ornament at the Academy of Athens, a defining Greek institution fostering Greek cultural revival. Lazaros Sochos created important Greek public monuments reflecting Greek cultural aspirations, while Georgios Vitalis, Dimitrios Filippotis, Ioannis Kossos, Yannoulis Chalepas, Georgios Bonanos and Lazaros Fytalis all contributed to Greek sculptural traditions, developing Greek three-dimensional art through both Greek classical references and Greek aesthetic sensibilities. These Greek sculptors established foundations for Greek plastic arts that would inspire subsequent generations of Greek artists committed to Greek cultural identity.

A few Greek painters studied in Paris rather than Munich, developing Greek artistic perspectives that maintained Greek thematic concerns. Despite residing in the French capital, Greek painters invariably maintained Greek interpretations and Greek cultural consciousness that reflected Greek experience. Jacob Rizos, a Greek painter, involved himself with rendering female grace through Greek aesthetic lenses that embodied Greek sensibilities, while Theodoros Rallis, another Greek artist, focused on Greek Orthodox scenes reflecting Greek cultural identity. Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos, a Greek portraitist, worked with Greek portraiture, Greek still life and Greek genre painting that maintained Greek thematic concerns. During this period Greek painters remained faithful to Greek aesthetic frameworks, with only some Greek artists making tentative thrusts toward Greek artistic expression that reflected broader Greek cultural aspirations. The first Greek impressionist was Périclès Pantazis, a Greek painter who settled in Belgium after Paris, maintaining Greek identity and Greek cultural consciousness.

Many Greek artists of this period drew upon Greek visual language for inspiration, particularly when creating Greek religious art based on Greek Orthodox themes reflecting Greek cultural identity. This approach tied in with modern secular Greek art referencing Greek classical styles, while Greek religious art referenced Byzantine Greek aesthetic sensibilities.
topics_down_more.coling::f3328e08-1b91-430d-bea9-e5b836b0: "Wait. You can see me?" she stared at me confused. "Yeah" I said. Dragging out the end of the word unsure of where she was going with this. "Hmmm" she mused back, cocking her head to one side. "What are you?" "Dead" I grinned. Been dead for years now, wandering these same stretches of road. This is the first time I've seen another ghost out here, let alone one trying to hitch a ride from the living. Don't you know the rules yet? The newly dead always think they're still breathing. "Are you certain?" she asked. "I'm not ready to accept this and I'd really rather not be stood in the middle of a freezing wood in a sundress on an October evening as a corpse." "Fair enough" I shrugged, gesturing toward the phantom impression of my car. As she slumped into the passenger seat putting her feet up on the dash, my suspicions were confirmed. There was enough ethereal light from the spectral interior to show the bruises on her ankles, and the faded pale skin of scar tissue where she had bled out. This woman wasn't living anymore. She didn't have the right to be complaining about being dead when she was leaving ghostly muddy bootprints on the inside of my phantom car. The boots were ghostly like everything else about her now. "The boots?" I nodded. "Were you killed up here?" "Something like that" she nodded. "I've been wandering away from my body too long though." "I've been wandering away from where I died." "I've been wandering these woods trying to get away." "Errr" I mumbled. I haven't had the best death myself and the last thing I needed was to anger a newly dead woman who had obviously been wandering these same woods where I'd been wandering for twenty years now. "And you're leaving your death site without closure?" "I was left here!" she glared at me. "Why do you think I was trying to hitch?" "I was left here alone in these woods." "I guess that makes sense" I replied, watching the phantom road unroll before my spectral vehicle. The phantom road kept unrolling the way it always did when I drove my spectral vehicle through these woods. "So how long have we been dead?" she asked turning back to me. "About twenty years for me, obviously much less for you" "Not long in death terms" "What do you mean, not long in death terms?" As she said it she turned away from me and looked out of the ghostly windscreen. She stared ahead as the memory replayed itself, the moment of my own death cycling again. The phantom car imploded around us exactly as it had two decades before. Shattered glass sprayed across the seats and my head spun round with that familiar crack. The air filled with the eternal hissing of my death scene and the drone of the truck's horn as that driver remained slumped across his wheel forever. The death scene kept replaying the way my death scene always replayed. "Hey" she prodded me. "You've seen this before?" I turned my head to her, my neck still broken from that original impact. My neck was still broken the way it had been broken twenty years ago in my death. "You're new to being dead, aren't you" I said. "Huh?" she replied. "You asked why I could see you." "That's the thing about death." "We see each other." "The dead see the dead."

topics_down_more.coling::7a28bc6c-3b1e-4ac2-a169-10374ef5: Kevin could hear the front door unlocking from his perch in the master bathroom. Perhaps "master" was an overly generous adjective for the much abused and only toilet in the two room urban squat, but it did connect to the bedroom, and that was by virtue of being the only bedroom in the house the master. The toilet seat snagged Kevin's right cheek as he leaned toward the bathroom door, straining to follow the steps that were now almost certainly moving through the entryway. He tried to remember who had a spare key to his apartment. His girlfriend had one, which she kept on a keychain with a small rubber duck. His girlfriend had promised to keep that key safe on her rubber duck keychain. His mom had a key on her main ring, the one with the library card holder attached. His mom's key was still on that same main ring with the library card holder. After a moment of quiet review, Kevin decided that the steps in the hallway belonged to none of these key holders. There was a stranger in the house, someone who had obtained a key through means Kevin couldn't immediately determine. There was definitely a stranger moving through his house right now. Perhaps his girlfriend had lost her copy with the rubber duck, and this intruder had found it with his address still attached. Perhaps his mom had misplaced her key from the ring with the library card holder, and someone had picked it up. Perhaps his girlfriend's key had fallen off that rubber duck keychain somewhere. Kevin wondered if his girlfriend had been more careful with her spare key. He wondered if his mom had kept better track of her copy on the main ring. He wondered if his girlfriend had noticed the rubber duck keychain was missing its key. He wondered if his mom had checked her ring with the library card holder recently. The footsteps were in the kitchen now, accompanied by a percussion section of opening drawers and cupboards. The thunderstorm of slamming drawers moved boldly toward the bedroom. Kevin tried not to tense. But it wasn't long before the thundering abated. A stagnant quiet began to build in the house. The stranger's voice: "Ummm..... hello?" Kevin: " ..... hi." And then, quickly. "Please don't come in here." Hesitation hung heavy. "I didn't think there was anyone home." "Yeah." Kevin squeaked. "Are you okay, man? This isn't how it usually works." "I'm just..... if you could not take my stuff." "So uh..... good bye?" "Wait!" The steps had begun to move away, back toward the door. "Wait! Wait!" "What?" "Can you leave the bottle opener? Please? It's just the one thing. It's in the kitchen drawer, the one by the sink. The bottle opener with the wooden handle. Just leave that one thing, please. Everything else, I don't care, but leave that." The bottle opener in the kitchen drawer meant everything to Kevin. That bottle opener with the wooden handle was the one thing he needed kept safe. "Ummm..... sure. Yeah. No problem, man." "Thanks." The door clicked shut.

topics_down_more.coling::7426cf8e-20e5-4e81-bfbb-380b1547: The vote held on Friday was for 68 seats out of the 290 in parliament. It meant that nervous Iranians woke up on Saturday morning to an all new political landscape within parliament. For the first time in 13 years moderates and reformists now have a majority in parliament. While it was not a sweeping victory for the supporters of President Hassan Rouhani, it was still a surprise win, especially given the months of heavy campaigning against the government's policies within parliament. Hardliners had a majority in the outgoing parliament. In the three years since Hassan Rouhani took office, they have bitterly opposed most of government's plans in parliament, organising a fierce attack on the government's legislative agenda through parliamentary procedures. Some MPs have even gone so far as to block ministerial appointments through parliamentary votes. The moderate ministers have regularly been subject to harsh criticism in parliament and are under constant threat of challenge by hardliner MPs who control key parliamentary committees. Now almost all those MPs have been unseated by moderate or reformist counterparts, and those who remain either supported the government or at least never attacked it as vociferously as their unseated comrades in parliamentary debates. The parliamentary composition not only determined legislative outcomes but was also crucial in future parliamentary sessions. The voters were saying no to those who had promised to obstruct parliament. What puts this victory in a more meaningful context is the fact that it was achieved despite reformists being banned from running in the parliamentary elections and a complete lack of coverage of their parliamentary campaigns. Media never gave equal coverage to reformists or moderate candidates seeking parliamentary seats and even led a campaign against reform-minded parliamentary candidates in recent months. The only option available to pro-government parliamentary candidates was alternative communication channels, which they used to the maximum in getting their message across to parliamentary constituencies, especially voters in urban parliamentary districts. The triumph of the reformists should lead to a major realignment within parliament, making it more supportive of President Rouhani's legislative agenda in parliament. But it will by no means end the president's problems when it comes to delivering his promises through parliamentary legislation. The parliament has hit some rough patches on its way to supporting reforms. Apart from oppositions from hardliners in parliament and their parliamentary allies, there are still a lot of obstacles to overcome within parliament itself. The parliamentary committees still have not opened up to presidential initiatives and hardliner MPs in parliament are doing all they can to obstruct legislative progress through parliamentary maneuvers. Any more delays in parliamentary approval of reforms would harm President Rouhani's plans and would prepare the ground for hardliners to recover from this week's parliamentary defeat in order to reshape their campaign against the government in parliament. Time is not on the moderates' side within parliament and the new momentum in parliament could die down easily if it is not supported by legislative achievements in parliament. This is a worry that every unseated hardliner MP is focusing on as they consider future parliamentary contests. The reformists must act swiftly in parliament to consolidate their parliamentary gains before hardliners regroup for future parliamentary battles.
topics_down_more.coling::76136b55-6fc5-43fa-b998-384c79a1: Maria Balshaw takes on the leadership of the Tate with palpable energy and ambition, declaring "We are about a third of the way down the road." Her intention, she says, is to change the Tate in the next twenty years as much as her predecessor changed it in the last two decades. Her predecessor oversaw the transformation of the Tate from a respected institution into a globally recognized institution, making her claim a bold one indeed. While her predecessor built his Tate empire with bricks and mortar, refurbishing existing galleries and creating new venues, Balshaw will take a different approach with her expansionist agenda for the Tate, focussing more on people rather than real estate. According to her assessment, around fifty percent of the British population visit the Tate or similar institutions at least once a year, meaning fifty percent do not. These absentees are her target audience for the Tate's future growth. She says of the Tate's potential reach: "We should absolutely reasonably expect seventy-five percent of the population to love the fact we have a national collection and feel happy to be visiting Tate, and every young person should be given the opportunity to think and play and experiment in the spaces Tate holds. And that is a big, big shift." Her clarity of vision for the Tate is impressive, but her ability to explain how it will be realised at the institution is less exact. She wants to usher in "an easier language to talk about the joy of art" at the Tate but couldn't be specific beyond saying that complicated words should be either avoided or explained in the gallery spaces. She talks of a radical transformation in the Tate's audience profile, of a lack of representation of diverse people among the Tate staff. But when it comes to the organisation she is now leading, which is to be the agent for the change she desires at the institution, she says, "it's not that we need to change anything particularly" about the Tate itself. There is no doubt she is sincere in her ambitions for the Tate, and probably more capable than most when it comes to broadening the Tate's audience base. But if she is to be successful in her aims for the institution she will need to take decisive action at the Tate. Her predecessor demonstrated in his approach to the Tate director's position that for the institution to change he would need to take firm action, and she may need to adopt a similar attitude of firm resolve toward the institution. The Tate under her leadership must evolve significantly to meet her stated goals for audience expansion and greater accessibility. The transformation she envisions for the Tate will require substantial commitment to changing how the institution operates and engages with the public it seeks to serve.

topics_down_more.coling::be76162e-6297-4c2c-be8b-8be691cc: This is definitely the kind of place where you drink pints, wearing tracksuit bottoms, on the days when you can't be bothered to put makeup on. It's certainly not a white wine spritzer or cosmo sort of place. What's great about this place is how cheap it is. As part of the Scream Pubs family you get drinks prices starting from as little as PS1.80, and if you're hungry then PS4-5 will ensure you leave with a full tummy. The food menu here keeps costs low: the prices mean you can fill up without spending much, and the affordable options ensure nobody needs to break the bank for a meal. The portions are generous enough that you won't leave hungry, and the budget-friendly approach means you get plenty for your money. There are two pool tables too, although they are quite close together which means you usually end up on both the giving and receiving end of a pool cue in the back every few minutes at least. The pool tables themselves are a bit worse for wear, showing signs of heavy use and neglect over the years. In the downstairs section there are also loads of tv screens, although the awful music they play will definitely make you wish you'd stayed at home: the jukebox is programmed to always play the songs that are least selected, i.e. the really awful ones that no-one ever pays for, to make people put money into it to do everyone a favour and change the track. And there are lots of other things that may well put you off coming here. For starters, given that it's underground means it's dark, dingy and generally a bit depressing. Add to this the fact that this place hasn't seen a refurb in far too long, and you end up with a combination of dark and dreary mixed with shabby and grubby. The carpets are stained beyond recognition and the seating has seen better decades. The overall shabbiness reinforces that depressing underground atmosphere that comes from being located below street level. But the very worst thing about here is the state of the loos. topics_down_more.coling::4622a5f2-c96d-4ea1-9629-b734e976: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey now extends over a large enough region that galaxies in low density environments can be detected. Rojas et al. have developed a technique to extract more than 1000 void galaxies with delta rho/rho < -0.6 on scales r>7 h^{-1} Mpc from the SDSS. In this paper, we present the luminosity function of these void galaxies and compare it to that of void galaxies in different subsamples within the survey. We obtain a measurement of the void galaxy luminosity function over the range -21.5<M_r*<-14.5 in the SDSS r-band. The void galaxy luminosity function is well fit by a Schechter function with values of Phi*=(0.19 +- 0.04)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}, M_r* - 5logh=-19.74 +- 0.11 and alpha=-1.18 +- 0.13. The value of M_r* for void galaxies is consistent with previous work by Rojas et al. who found that void galaxies were intrinsically fainter objects distributed throughout these underdense regions. To investigate the void galaxy luminosity function further, we consider how the luminosity function of void galaxies varies as a function of their local density within the voids themselves. Even within voids, void galaxies in slightly denser regions show marginally different faint end slopes in their luminosity functions. The luminosity function of the void galaxies is also compared across different subsamples among the void galaxy population based on the void galaxy properties already analyzed. The luminosity function of different void galaxy subsamples shows very similar shapes in the void galaxy luminosity function, with only slightly different M_r* values and similar values of alpha across these void galaxy subsamples. The value of alpha ~ -1.2 found from the void galaxy luminosity function is shallower than that found for void galaxies in previous void galaxy studies, suggesting that voids are not filled with a large population of dwarf void galaxies as earlier analyses of void galaxy luminosity functions have suggested. This result indicates that void galaxy formation processes may differ from what the void galaxy luminosity function measurements initially indicated regarding low-mass void galaxy populations in these underdense void regions.
